Minister): Mr. Speaker, on this day of "St. John the Baptist", may I associate myself with my French speaking fellow Canadians to pay tribute to their patron saint and to again recall in this parliament the contribution of French Canadians to our national life in all its aspects.
I should like to draw a lesson from the life of St. John the Baptist, who was beheaded for his indefectible courage in the defence of freedom and in denouncing the ways of the tyrant of the day. Today, when as a result of the historic evolution of peoples, western nations are faced with the task of defending man's fundamental freedoms, all Canadians need to feel united and draw from their traditions the courage and inspiration required to overcome the problems that may arise and hamper their common efforts for the establishment of a strong and prosperous nation, and full development of all its resources and possibilities.

Mr. Speaker, like the Prime Minister, I should like also to call the attention of the house to an important event in the life of French Canadians: the celebration of St. John the Baptist day, in honour of their patron saint. Throughout French Canada, this feast day is celebrated with joy and enthusiasm. Not only in the province of Quebec are there joyous demonstrations-especially in Montreal, that big city, where is staged every year a parade of floats-to stress the importance of this patron saint's day, but also elsewhere in Canada.
I am just back from western Canada and in Gravelbourg, Saskatchewan, St. John the
Baptist day was being celebrated this year. In Cornwall, Ontario, the French week will conclude with the celebration of St. John the Baptist day.
Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate that our patron saint's day should thus be celebrated because its purpose is to show that French Canadians are strongly attached to their language and religion. As long as our two cultures, the French and the English, can flourish without hindrance, we will have unity and peace, because they are the prerequisites of the progress and development of the whole country.
I should also like to call attention to the anniversary of the discovery of Newfoundland of which the Prime Minister spoke a few minutes ago. On this occasion, we should like to associate ourselves with our fellow citizens of that province and offer them our best wishes.

I wish to reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Essex East concerning the supply of munitions to Portugal.

of recommendations from the central NATO military and civilian authorities.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in line with my usual practice I propose to make a brief general statement in opening the committee's consideration of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
As hon. members will note from the blue book, we are budgeting for a total expenditure in the fiscal year 1961-62 of approximately $1,600 million. This represents an increase of close to $150 million or roughly 10 per cent over the previous 12-month period. A customary feature of the department's annual spending program is the predominance of statutory expenditures. This is again apparent in our proposed outlays for 1961-62, in which statutory items amount to about $1,500 million or 94 per cent of the grand total.
Here the main components are: $606,600,000 for payments required under the Old Age Security Act; $523 million for payments required under the Family Allowances Act; $270 million for the federal share of costs under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act; $45,100,000 for federal contributions under the Unemployment Assistance Act; $30,900,000 for payments to the provinces under the Old Age Assistance Act; $16,600,000 for payments to the provinces under the Disabled Persons Act; and $4,200,000 for payments to the provinces under the Blind Persons Act.
Such statutory items account, as I have said, for 94 per cent of our projected total outlays for the fiscal year 1961-62. The remaining 6 per cent or $96 million represents items to be voted by parliament. These include: $47 million for payments to the provinces under the national health grants; $25 million for Indian and northern health services; $8 million for emergency health, welfare and training services; $3,700,000 for quarantine, immigration medical and sick mariners services; $2,300,000 for administration of the Food and Drugs Act; and $2,400,000 for laboratory and advisory services.
Looking at the increase in departmental outlays for 1961-62, statutory items account for $141,100,000 of the $150 million total increase. By far the most important factor is an additional $103 million required for the hospital insurance and diagnostic services program. This is to take care of anticipated increases in expenditures including the first full year of federal contributions under the agreement signed with the province of Quebec which became operative on January

Supply-Health and Welfare 1, 1961. The remaining $38,100,000 increase will cover the normal year to year growth of the various statutory welfare benefits which are paid either fully by the dominion government or on a sharing basis with the provinces.
Of the over-all $8,900,000 increase in voted items, $5 million relates to the national health grants and chiefly to the acceleration of hospital construction projects. The $2,600,000 increase in emergency health, welfare and training services is required largely for completion of phase 1 of the transportable hospital program. The net increase of $590,000 for Indian and northern health services is associated with the further expansion of services provided by that directorate.
This, then, is the broad outline of the department's spending program for the fiscal year 1961-62 which, as I have pointed out, totals close to $1,600 million. As hon. members are aware, there are a number of important policy steps which have recently been implemented in connection with my department. These include a new narcotic control act, an amendment to the Food and Drugs Act with reference to the so-called goof ball problem, and the announcement of the membership and terms of reference of the royal commission on health care.
In this regard, it has been most gratifying to the government to note the generally favourable reaction which these steps have evoked throughout the country. This is particularly evident in relation to the comprehensiveness of the study outlined in the terms of reference of the royal commission. On this point, we have felt that it would be unwise to attempt to examine any particular aspect in isolation, since health services are interdependent and must be closely integrated.
For example, the committee will note that the terms of reference not only envisage a close study of health services but also focus attention on the importance of training of professional and technical personnel and related medical research. This is to ensure that health services in Canada keep pace with developments in medical science which in turn will provide the highest possible quality of health care for all Canadians.
As far as the commission itself is concerned, I know the committee will welcome the fact that such a distinguished group of Canadians have been willing to set aside their ordinary activities in order to serve the country in a matter of such great importance. Under the chairmanship of Chief Justice Hall I am sure the study will proceed with all possible dispatch.
I should like to say a few words about the hospital insurance and diagnostic services


program, which is now in operation throughout Canada. As hon. members will recall, the twelfth and final agreement was signed with the province of Quebec in December, 1960 and became effective January 1, 1961. While not all the provinces have as yet fully implemented the federal legislation with respect to insured out-patient services, we have reached the stage where some 18 million Canadians are eligible for coverage for basic in-patient hospital and diagnostic services.
From the point of view of my department, our estimated contribution to provincial programs for 1961-62 is $270 million. This, as I said, represents an increase of $103 million over the original estimate for 1960-61. The bulk of the increase is due, of course, to the fact that the province of Quebec, with a population of some 5,200,000, will be participating for the first time over a full 12-month period. Federal advances in this regard have been set at something over $72 million. In addition, an allowance has to be made for the final adjustment with the provinces for the calendar years 1959 and 1960, as well as for expected rises in costs associated with such factors as increasing bed utilization owing to increased numbers of hospital beds and growing population.
If I might be permitted to go back to the fiscal year 1960-61 for a moment, the house will recall that our original estimate of federal contributions was $167 million. As things turned out, this was on the low side. It did not include, for example, the participation of Quebec during the first three months of 1961 which, of course, could not have been foreseen when the calculations were made. This has involved federal outlays of some $13,900,000. When allowance is also made for increases in the cost of hospital operations generally, the total federal contribution for 1960-61 amounted to $189 million.
I turn now to the national health grants. Hon. members will note a change in their presentation in the blue book. For 1961-62 they have been split up into two separate votes, general health grants and hospital construction grants. Formerly they were all under one vote but under separate headings. The new arrangement, I would point out, is merely for greater administrative convenience. As the committee is aware, there are certain differences between hospital construction grants and the other grants, particularly the fact that funds outstanding under the former are subject to annual revote while those under the latter lapse at the end of each fiscal year. In view of such considerations, it has been felt more appropriate to have them appear under separate votes.
I wish to say a word now about polio vaccine. The dominion government has, of

course, played an important part in the nation-wide Salk immunization program. Some $6 million in federal funds has been contributed toward the cost of producing the vaccine, and the same kind of support is now being given the development in Canada of the new Sabin-type live polio virus vaccine. This oral vaccine is being manufactured in Canada at the Connaught medical research laboratories in Toronto, and plans are under way at the institute of microbiology and hygiene in Montreal for similar production. Federal financial support in this regard has already amounted to over $250,000. While it is still too early to assess the results of various demonstrations conducted in different parts of Canada, indications so far have been favourable. Because, however, of certain technical difficulties, licensing of the vaccine is still a matter which is under review.
Another development in connection with my department's health activities merits brief mention. This was the opening on January 16, 1961 of a new 80-bed general hospital at Inuvik, Northwest Territories. Costing close to $2 million, the hospital provides an important additional link in our far flung services for Indians, Eskimos, and other residents of the north. It will cover primarily the Mackenzie river delta, and brings to 22 the total number of hospitals operated by our Indian and northern health services.
On the welfare side of my department's operations, it will be noted that this continues to account for the great bulk of our annual expenditures. In fact cash benefit programs such as family allowances, old age security and various joint federal-provincial pension arrangements add up to $1,200 million out of our total budget of $1,600 million.
For 1961-62 our expenditures for old age security are expected to reach some $600 million. This substantial amount is due not only to the steady increase in the number of recipients but also to the higher rate of benefits paid now as compared with the amount provide at the time the program was inaugurated. Indeed, of the amount now involved, approximately $165 million is due to the increase in benefits from $40 to $55 a month.
A further point worth mentioning is the current state of the old age security fund. In the fiscal year just completed, revenues from the three earmarked taxes were sufficient to meet benefit payments. For the first time in the history of the program it was not necessary to resort to loans to make up a deficit. This is a most encouraging development, and means that old age security has at last achieved the original objective of financing on a pay as you go basis.

As hon. members will recall, an important change was introduced in the program last year. I refer to the new provision permitting qualified old age security recipients to draw pensions while residing outside Canada even on a permanent basis. This move was very well received throughout the country and has, I believe, been of substantial value to many pensioners who for one reason or another have chosen to leave Canada.
It is interesting to note the number of persons who have taken advantage of the amendment. As of April 30, 1961, 6,758 pensioners were receiving old age security benefits out of the country. This represents three quarters of 1 per cent of the total number benefiting under the program. Of these out of country recipients, 1,357 were residing in the United Kingdom, 4,536 in the United States and 865 in other countries of the world. As I have pointed out the legislation now permits payments to qualified pensioners who are absent indefinitely. According to our latest figures, 2,777 pensioners have been away from Canada beyond the period of six months. This is one third of 1 per cent of the total number of recipients.
At this point it might be of interest to see where Canada stands in relation to other federal states of the western world in the matter of cash benefits for senior citizens. In 1959-60 our expenditures, including old age security and old age assistance, represented 2.45 per cent of the net national income. In the same year, payments in Australia accounted for 2.33 per cent of national income and in the United States for 2.66 per cent. The latter includes both the O.A.S.I. and old age assistance programs. This small differential between the United States and Canada is particularly significant when you consider that per capita personal income in the United States is almost a third higher than in Canada.
Before leaving the matter of benefits for senior citizens I should perhaps add that the government is continuing its examination of various approaches to old age income security. This includes of course matters such as portable pensions, the Clark report, and developments in other countries. In view of the growing interest on the part of labour, management and a number of provinces in the provision of more adequate private pension arrangements, this area has been receiving particular consideration. As hon. members are aware, the Minister of Finance in his latest budget statement indicated that the government has decided to ask the cooperation of the provinces to deal with the solvency and portability of private pension plans. We consider that there is room for

Supply-Health and Welfare more widespread expansion of these plans on a secure basis, and are prepared to work with the provinces toward this end.
A survey which is now being carried out by the dominion bureau of statistics should prove to be of particular value in connection with this latest proposal. This survey will provide up to date data on the number of persons covered under private pension plans, the nature and extent of vesting and cash surrender provisions, as well as information on the transferability of pension rights. These and other facts relating to private provisions for old age income security should prove most helpful in any federal-provincial discussions on this subject.
I might also say a word or two about the unemployment assistance program. As I mentioned earlier, our estimated expenditures in this regard amount to some $45 million for the current fiscal year. Since claims by the provinces for federal reimbursement may be as much as six months late in reaching my department, it is not possible to provide up to date figures as to the number receiving benefits under the program. In October, 1960, however, it appears that the total coverage had reached something over 400,000 persons including dependents.
The increase in expenditures under unemployment assistance over the past few years has been due to a number of factors. Among these are the program's extension to all provinces and the territories, the removal of the threshold provision and the increase in rates of benefits paid by the provinces and municipalities. In addition, there is the fact that a number of provinces, including Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, are now using the program to provide supplementary relief payments to recipients of old age security, old age assistance, blindness and disability allowances. This means in effect that the dominion government has been sharing in additional aid above the general level of $55 a month, which in cases of special need has not constituted a rigid ceiling on benefit payments.
I do not plan to make any remarks at this time with regard to the fitness, recreation and amateur sports program forecast in the speech from the throne and which, as the Prime Minister mentioned in answer to a question in the house recently, will be dealt with through legislation. An opportunity will be provided for detailed consideration of this subject when the matter is brought before the house.
Finally I should like to turn to our efforts in emergency planning and radiation protection. Earlier this year cabinet approval was given for the establishment of a special


advisory committee to the Minister of National Health and Welfare on emergency health services. Like its predecessor, the defence medical and dental services advisory board, this committee is composed of the appropriate federal officials as well as representatives of various national health organizations. Its first meeting took place here in Ottawa last month, and I am glad to say that a good start was made toward providing greater stimulus and continuity to the progress of emergency health planning in Canada.
As in the case of emergency health activities, the greatest problem in emergency welfare planning has been to encourage the setting up of suitable organizations within provincial departments. I am therefore happy to inform the house that arrangements have now been worked out with nine provinces, including the appointment of five provincial emergency welfare service planning officers to be paid under the financial assistance program. Taken together with the increasing coordination of policy and stepped-up training activities, this development, I believe, augurs well for the continued growth of Canada's capability to meet whatever emergency welfare needs may arise in the years ahead.
On the matter of radiation protection, I have indicated on previous occasions that preparations were under way for what is called a total body monitor unit. The physical facilities for the unit have now been completed and the necessary equipment and special steel shielding installed. When in full operation the total body monitor will constitute a major addition to our over-all radiation measurements program.
Other aspects of our radiation protection activities have continued to expand to meet the increasing demand for services. A network of 23 stations has been set up across Canada for the regular collection of samples of air, rainfall and soil. The well established milk sampling program is going ahead, and we are also beginning to receive human bone samples in accordance with a revised sampling pattern. The results of all of these studies are published in quarterly and annual reports.
In this connection, the latest figures on strontium-90 in milk bear out our expectation of declining levels. For the fourth quarter of 1960 the national average was 9.5 micromicrocuries per gram calcium compared with 15, 12.9 and 9.3 during the previous three quarters of 1960. These levels are all the more significant when it is recalled that the quarterly figures for 1959 were 10.8, 18, 14.6 and 14.2 respectively.
During the past 12 months additional laboratory facilities have been provided for the

analysis of radioactive samples from foreign countries. This, as hon. members will recall, was planned as Canada's contribution to the world-wide fall-out study program of the United Nations scientific committee on the effects of atomic radiation. In this connection negotiations have been under way with four countries, Ghana, Pakistan, Burma and Malaya. Agreement in principle has now been reached with the first three, while discussions with the fourth are still in process.
Just before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I should like to pay a tribute to the staff of the Department of National Health and Welfare who have assisted me during the past year, many of whom have been in the department for many years, and to their dedication to duty during that period. I should also like to mention that yesterday morning I had the pleasure of turning the sod for a new headquarters building at Tunney's pasture. This will bring units now scattered in some 19 different locations throughout Ottawa under one roof for the first time, and while it is going to take some two years to complete the building I am sure that the new headquarters will lend itself to much more efficiency in the management of the department.

Mr. Chairman, no one regrets more than I the unavoidable absence this morning of the former minister of national health and welfare, the member for Essex East, by reason of a previous commitment. In these late days of the session we have very little advance notice, of course, which departmental estimates will be discussed on Saturdays. So it falls to me today, as it did two years ago, I believe, under similar circumstances involving short notice, to make some observations on behalf of the official opposition in connection with the department's program and comment upon the statements made by the minister in introducing his estimates for 1961-62.
I was a bit disappointed by his presentation. This is a terrifically important department of government from the point of view of human benefit and advancement. The minister did not say so, but in recent years it has been the second largest spending department of the government. The minister also did not say so, but I suspect that in the coming year it may perhaps overtake the Department of National Defence as the biggest spending department. Although the minister indicated that over 94 per cent of the department's expenditures result from prior statutory decisions and are not policy matters that come before us for consideration at this time, the fact is that new advances require legislation and the minister has not given
Supply-Health and Welfare us any indication that such new legislation is being planned by the department.
In my opinion he confined himself too much to a financial and statistical analysis of the department. In a department of this kind I would have thought we might have had from the minister an indication that the department is not standing still, that it has studies actively under way beyond those to which he referred, which were not very many in number, that would involve new programs which would indicate that the department was continuing to provide inspiring and imaginative leadership in welfare and health arenas. I regret that in the report the minister made in introducing his estimates there was nothing with respect to the views of the department on a comprehensive medical health plan.
Respecting pensions, we have heard from the minister every two months during the past two years in which he has had the Clark report in his possession that he has been studying this report. He said nothing more about it in his presentation today.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, studying it; and, as I have said, the minister has made similar statements every two months over the past two years.
All of us receive copies of the representations that are made to the cabinet each year by the Canadian welfare council, and we note the many imaginative and advanced programs set out therein. The minister made no reference to the attitude of the government toward the representations made by this most competent, most dedicated, voluntary organization. A resolution was introduced during this session by the hon. member for Mount Royal respecting the problem of mental health. At that time the minister said he had a great deal of sympathy for the purport of the resolution. This is another important field in which no report was given to the nation by the minister during the introduction of his estimates.
Earlier this session I raised a question with regard to Canada's participation in an important conference held in Washington relating to medical care for the aged. We have heard no reference to that. If the government is not prepared to embark upon a comprehensive medical plan, are there no studies under way in respect of medical assistance at least for the aged? There was some reference in the minister's statement to portable pensions. The Ontario government has had a committee at work in this field, and this committee believes a central agency should undertake consideration of portable and trans-

Supply-Health and Welfare ferable pensions. This subject was mentioned in the budget speech, and reference was made to the fact that it is merely under study and that the participation of the provinces is required.
The minister mentioned the old age security fund. He said that, for the first time, the fund was in balance. We all know that in 1959 new taxes were imposed on the income tax side, on the excise tax side and on the corporation tax side which were designed to bring in from the point of view of tax imposts $2 for every dollar to which the government had committed itself in extra payments under old age security in the previous year.
The minister gave some illustrations of the percentage of national expenditure applied in some countries in the health and welfare field. He compared Canada's position in this respect to that of the United States, Australia and some other countries. There is a feeling in Canada and the United States, particularly among businessmen, that one of the handicaps from which they suffer in competing in world markets is the fact that we have an unnecessarily heavy burden of welfare payments.
I have been looking at some reports recently provided by the Canadian tax foundation. I was startled to realize that this impression that is held and spread by many Canadian businessmen to the effect that they cannot compete in export markets because of the tax burden imposed by welfare payments is not borne out by the facts. I find that, on the tax side, our taxes are not higher than those imposed by the countries of western Europe and Britain from which our businessmen are getting the keenest competition. On the welfare side, the tax foundation reports that the welfare payments of those countries take a greater percentage of the national income than is the situation in either Canada or the United States. We must not excuse our failure to compete in the markets of the world with countries such as Germany and the other keen, aggressive countries in western Europe by saying that we pay higher taxes in Canada, or that government legislation in Canada and the United States imposes upon the business community the cost of welfare payments beyond those of our competitors in western Europe. These are not the facts.
The minister referred to unemployment assistance. I hope later, during the discussion of his estimates, we will hear much more about this subject. It is true that $45 million will be required under this program, according to the estimates which are before us. The minister said that in October, 1960 some

400,000 Canadians participated in the unemployment assistance provided by this legislation. He said that this resulted from a number of factors. He quoted some liberalization of the rules under which the federal department participates with the provinces and, in turn, with the municipalities in this field. Of course one would not expect the minister to mention what I believe to be the fundamental factor, that such a huge number participated. I pointed out the reason for this condition the other day in the budget debate, when I referred to the complacency and lack of planning on the part of this government which has resulted in a lack of proper growth in our economy, a stagnation which has meant that the gross national product has not increased in the same way it has in other countries throughout the world to take care of those who are entering our labour force.
I remind the members of the committee that as recently as last year the estimates committee spent 20 sittings studying the program and expenditures of this Department of National Health and Welfare. I was a member of that committee. I felt the review was very rewarding indeed. The Hansard record of the estimates committee covers over 500 pages, and as a result of that review last year perhaps we will be able to shorten the debate today in this committee of supply of the House of Commons.
However, I want to refer again to what I think is the most important next step that must be considered by those in the Department of National Health and Welfare. I refer, of course, to a comprehensive medical plan. We have had a short experience now with the hospital insurance plan. However, hospitalization insurance alone falls short. I think all national political parties have been giving this matter considerable attention. Better programs are available in other countries. However, I wish to put on the record the up to date plan the Liberal party proposes in this field. In doing so may I say that I am quoting from the resolution presented and approved unanimously at its rally in January, 1961:
Second only to the threat of unemployment is the threat of illness. Hospital insurance, which has now become available to all Canadians, does much to lessen the insecurity of ill health. But it is not enough. Many people still face medical costs outside the hospital scheme, that are financially crippling to them. While various good schemes of prepaid medical care are in operation, they are not available to everyone, on terms everyone can afford. In consequence there are still many Canadians who go without medical care that they need; and others, whom serious illness forces to go to a doctor are thereby pushed into overwhelming debt or a catastrophic impairment of their savings.

It is the Liberal policy to end such social evils. Universal hospital insurance was a big step forward. Further measures are needed to reduce the insecurity arising from illness. A new Liberal government will undertake at once, to provide extended hospital facilities including mental health and rehabilitation, comprehensive care by doctors, drugs and medicines and diagnostic services.
Now the question arises, how is this plan going to be paid for? This, of course, was questioned when we were still dealing with the supplementary budget of the Minister of Finance in January after the rally of the Liberal party. Nothing could be clearer as to the Liberal party's position in this respect than what was stated by the Leader of the Opposition on January 20, 1961 when those on the government side questioned the financial responsibility that was involved in a program of this kind. As found at page 1273 of Hansard the Leader of the Opposition gave four fiscal measures which he felt were being neglected and were of imperative concern after more immediate actions such as dealing with unemployment. He referred to reduction of the rates of personal income tax. He referred to extra unemployment benefits and some other matters. But with respect to the allembracing plan for health he said this; that perhaps the most important of those things that must come forward as needed new programs for Canadians is the matter of a medical health plan. The leader of this party said that this, of course, is one of those things that should be implemented during an expanding economy and not a contracting economy. Under the present government we have had five deficits in succession. Under the previous administration we were able to provide surpluses and reduce our debt. Under circumstances such as these, on a deficit financing basis, of course, perhaps it is not possible to finance the substantial costs of a medical health plan. However, given policies that would return us to surpluses in our financial administration I say, as did the Leader of the Opposition, that this would be one of the first of the new measures that should be added to Canada's health and welfare program.

As for the measures forecast to increase old age security and other social benefits, naturally every true Liberal will welcome them in principle. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to start off by doing something that I think I always try to do, namely by giving credit where credit is due and, of course, to criticize where we feel criticism is warranted. I should like to pay tribute to the sincerity of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I have always found him to take his duties very seriously and to discharge them very sincerely. I should also like to pay tribute to the devotion to duty of the members of his department. Because of the fact that the departments are so closely intertwined and interwoven I also pay a special tribute to the provincial department of health and welfare in Ontario and to the deputy minister, Mr. James S. Band, with whom I have had occasion to have considerable dealings in connection with individual problems in the field of health and welfare.
For four years the party to which I belong has been critical of the policies of the present minister, as we were critical of the policies of the previous government during their term of office. With all due respect to my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River, for whom

Supply-Health and Welfare I have a very high regard, I do not think we can take the Liberal promises any more seriously today than we could when I was two years old and they promised us health insurance. However, in my few remarks today, in the interests of getting this extended session drawn that much closer to a close I intend to try to make a technical, at least in my humble opinion, rather than a political criticism of this situation.
If the C.C.F. party has for many years criticized this particular field it is because we feel that as a nation possibly this has been our greatest failure. In this very favoured country in which we live this is one field in which we lag far, far behind so many countries throughout the world. It is interesting to note that recently we have been joined in our criticism of the present methods and policies in connection with health and welfare by an ever growing number of people and newspapers throughout the country.
I should like to draw particular attention to the Globe and Mail of May 10, 1961. The whole of page 7 of this newspaper is devoted to this very problem. I think some of the things stated on this page might very well be placed on Hansard while we are debating this issue today. There is, for example, an article written Professor Kenneth Duncan, who is in the department of economic and political science, University of Western Ontario. I think some of his words are very apropos to the item before the committee. He says:
Welfare and social services provided to needy Canadians should be rationally organized and entirely financed from the public purse. In every province-and the province is the effective jurisdictional unit-these services are now provided by ill co-ordinated, overlapping, understaffed and underfinanced congeries of private and public agencies.
This ramshackle structure is a heritage from a time when all seemed to agree that it was no part of the government's duty to do much to comfort the afflicted. Most charity and social service work was then regarded as a matter for religious bodies, personal philanthropy or private organizations of the tender minded. It was in such a day that some of our best known and most useful agencies were founded.
A little later in his article he says:
Today, we find every level of government providing a variety of services or welfare payments such as family allowance, mother's allowance, old age assistance, public relief, medical care of the indigent, treatment for alcoholics, blind pensions etc. Yet public authorities were always willing to permit private agencies to go on providing services since it kept down taxes-
I should like to digress for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to underline that point. I have mentioned this on many occasions in the house. This is one of the fields in which we like to indulge in our favourite pastime of self-delusion. We feel that as long as we can

keep taxes down the government are doing a good job in this field, when in fact they are failing and are remiss in their duties. By virtue of keeping taxes down they do not provide these services and in fact, as is mentioned in this article, through a conglomeration of various agencies the cost to the public is actually higher than it would be if these agencies were properly organized. Professor Duncan goes on to say:
-and there remains as a consequence a complex of private agencies providing such things as child care and protection, family counselling, nursing and health services, care of homeless and transient men, protection of unwed mothers and numerous other services which by contemporary standards are necessary to the community.
Such an arrangement as this leads almost inevitably to inefficiency in operation, poor inter-agency co-ordination, high costs in terms of services given and to some abuse by professional indigents. It has persisted this long because each private agency inevitably becomes a vested interest.
I think that is one of our greatest problems in trying to get something done in this field. Over the years we have seen so many fields in the many different branches that make up the Department of Health and Welfare. We have seen these little, vested interests grow up in our society, and once they have grown up they dig in their heels and resist all efforts to improve the over-all situation because it interferes with their own particular organization.
In saying this I am not being critical of the individual organizations as such. Many good people devote many hours of hard work in order to make a success of their particular organizations. However, I think if we look at the over-all picture we see that the headline on this page is very well warranted. The headline reads:
Is full government control the answer to the failure of our welfare agencies?
That is being very critical of the present situation of the various health and welfare agencies in our society, but I think the criticism is very much warranted because if governments were doing the job they are capable of doing and should be doing in the first place, we would not need this great conglomeration of agencies be they religious, service club, private or what have you. The only reason these have sprung up across the country and have grown is that there was a great need in this field. I fully appreciate that at one time the thinking was that governments had no responsibility in this field, but I do not think we will find too many people in the country today who will go along with that type of thinking.
On the same page of this issue of the Globe and Mail there is another article written by a man who is very well known in this field, Professor John S. Morgan, who is

in the school of social work of the University of Toronto. The first paragraph of his article is, I think, well worth mentioning at this time. It reads:
The time has come to bring welfare up to date. Too many of us think of welfare as something that the rich provide for the poor or the wise give to the foolish. In actual fact, in a modern industrial society, all of us are recipients of welfare services and all of us contribute in some way to the provision of welfare services. The problem of welfare in the future is to organize the complex operations of this mutual dependency in the most effective, the most economical and the most efficient way.
I think the minister could do much worse than give a great deal of thought to the words of Professor Morgan. He is well known as one of the experts in this particular field on the North American continent. On the same page there is another article written by a gentleman who is becoming well known and who certainly is well versed in his own field. I am not going to deal with some of the most bitter criticisms in his article, because I think I could go as far as to say there may even be a political twist to this. I know the gentleman very well; he originally came from my own town of Timmins. This is an article written by Mr. Gower Markle, who is the Canadian director of education and welfare for the united steel workers of America. I should like to read one paragraph which I think is apropos of my remarks today. This paragraph reads as follows:
Much of the current debate on welfare is on the level of "who will give and how much" and "who will receive and how much". This serves only to obscure the fact that Canadians have yet to make a fundamental decision whether we are socially responsible or not. And if the answer is negative all the rest becomes irrelevant.
If the answer is positive-then, we have to determine how best to provide the goods and services required to take care of the present needy.
I should like now to highlight one matter which I believe to be a great problem and drawback in our efforts to develop some kind of sensible, comprehensive health and welfare program across this country. This problem involves a tendency on the part of many individuals and newspapers to look only at the actual cost in dollars involved in the development of a program upon which the government, through the Department of National Health and Welfare could embark, and completely ignore the resulting savings from the adoption of measures of this kind. They also completely ignore the better health standards that accrue from the adoption of such measures.
Another drawback to our efforts in this regard is the tendency on the part of governments, both federal and provincial, to boast about the number of dollars spent in certain fields, as though by the mere mention of the
Supply-Health and Welfare amount spent the job is accomplished. I suggest it is time to look at our health and welfare measures in the light of what has been accomplished and what has yet to be done rather than by just totalling up on an adding machine the X number of dollars which have already been spent.
We in this group for many years have propounded the need in this country of a portable pension plan. I have mentioned before one of the biggest obstacles to the accomplishment of this type of plan and do not intend to deal with it at length today. However, I should like to say that the obstacle arises because of the fact that over the years we have built up little groups of vested interests with pension plans, such as in industry and in municipalities, here and there and all over. In fact we have heard a great deal within the last few days about one pension plan, and we shall probably hear quite a bit more about it within the next few days.
Have we ever stopped to think that even this particular controversial pension plan of the past, present, but not too far in the future, governor of the Bank of Canada would involve no issue at the present time if it were part of a portable pension plan available to all citizens of this country? I believe this controversial pension plan will provide approximately 50 per cent of the governor's salary on retirement. I think that is a very laudable objective in respect to a comprehensive portable pension plan available to all citizens. I believe that if citizens of this country, from the governor of the Bank of Canada down, were to contribute their just and equitable share toward that type of a pension plan there would be no beef regarding anyone receiving 50 per cent of his salary on retirement, because each and every person in this country would then have paid an equitable share toward this pension to be received at retirement age.
Whenever we hear about pension plans, just as when we hear about health or hospital insurance plans, while we believe they are wonderful ideas we wonder where the money is to come from to pay for them. I should like to remind hon. members that a portable pension plan, such as I have referred to, should in the long run be self-liquidating and self-supporting. I agree that to establish a plan of this kind will involve the spending of a good deal of money for some time; but what we will be doing is paying off our past shortcomings, and once we have done so the plan will carry itself and there will be no cost as such then to the Canadian taxpayer.
I do not for one moment think this will be an easy task. I have given considerable study to the problem and realize the tremendous complexities involved. My greatest

Supply-Health and Welfare criticism of this government at the present time arises because I see no effort being made to reach this goal. This goal cannot be reached in six months or perhaps even in five years, but I maintain that if we never start, the job will never be done.
I fail to see any real measure of progress being made in this field by the present government, although it has been in office for four years. I believe this government should launch boldly on a plan, giving a complete and honest picture of the costs and prospects to the Canadian public. If this were done I am sure the public across the country would get behind the program and support it. If the taxpayers realized that by paying their proper share they could accomplish this job; if they knew they would not be hounded every Saturday morning by organizations carrying out tag days, which will not accomplish the job but only keep things going, they would support the government's program. I suggest that if the businessmen of this country knew that through the paying of proper taxes the job could be accomplished without their being hounded, not only on street corners during tag days but through their businesses and service clubs, which have never been able to accomplish the job in this country, the government would then get the full support of all those taxpayers, and this great program could be accomplished.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like previous speakers I should like to acknowledge the responsible manner in which the minister and his senior officials have discharged their responsibilities to parliament and to the country, and I should like to assure him that the small bouquets I throw do not contain any hidden bricks.
The previous speaker in his concluding remarks mentioned the undesirable feature of people wandering the streets on Saturdays holding tag days. While his remarks are prominently in my mind I should like to state that I do not think anyone in this country would stop publicly minded citizens from endeavouring to make their communities better places in which to live, or from helping their fellow citizens. I do not think this type of argument should be entertained in respect to this particular subject.
At the beginning of the present session I placed a resolution on the order paper which I hoped would have been discussed before this time. I regret that in referring to it now I am taking up some of the time for the discussion of the minister's estimates, but I feel that I should do so. That resolution requested the government to give early consideration to the advisability of instituting a contributory


pension system available to age 65 as a more equitable means of supporting the independence of Canadian senior citizens.
My purpose in bringing this resolution before the house and the country stems from my personal realization of the desire of most Canadians for such legislation and, I assure the committee, from my own humanitarian ideals, divorced completely from any political implications.
I believe that the three political parties now constituting the house agree unanimously that some such program should be instituted. I hold in my hand a press clipping of a statement by the hon. member for Essex East, who expressed a desire for such a plan. I have a statement by the Prime Minister which may not deal directly with it, but the inference one gathers from the statement is that the Prime Minister favours such a plan. I also have the statement made by the Minister of Finance when he presented his budget. This statement is taken out of context, of course, and has a slightly different meaning, but his words are as follows:
It is desirable that those who have been employed throughout their working years should be able to retire without fear of want.
I have a further statement by the minister of public welfare for the province of Ontario, part of which reads as follows:
In almost every country a contributory insurance-maintenance plan anticipates the future needs of these persons. We could view this as a responsibility which should be treated by the individual, himself. We might consider that he should prepare, well in advance, for his own future needs and the needs of his family-for the eventualities which will probably arise.
These are the important words:
Experience has shown, however, that such individual preparation does not take place.
When we hear the minister relate that 7,934,374 individuals collect $1,226,400,000 from the federal treasury I believe the wishes of the people should be given consideration in regard to the proposal I am making.
When I decided to discuss this matter in the house I immediately realized that the entire subject is too vast and complicated to discuss specifically. However, I hope the basis of my thoughts will be sufficiently clear to convince the minister, the government and all hon. members of the desirability of such a plan. Social security, as we refer to it, is by no means new to the world at large. I was interested in an excerpt from the book I hold in my hand, written by Mr. Arthur Larson, who is now director of the world rule of law centre at Duke University, North Carolina. This is the excerpt I should like to read:
It Is always something of a shock to those who call social security "socialistic" to discover that

it was, in origin, an anti-socialistic measure. It is an even worse shock to find that the father of social security was no dewy eyed liberal or left winger, but the iron chancellor himself-Otto von Bismarck.
During the years following the war of 18701871, Bismarck began to be concerned about the growing strength shown in elections by the Marxian socialists-whom we would now call communists. He met the situation, and took the wind out of the Marxians' sails, by laying before the Reichstag a comprehensive social insurance system. It was enacted in various measures between 1883 and 1887, and contained provisions for payments in case of sickness, accident, disability, widowhood, and old age.
The idea spread gradually throughout Europe, and received an important addition when the British, in 1911, added the idea of unemployment insurance. Once more, it is significant that it was not socialists or even trade unions who put through unemployment insurance in England. In fact, the Fabian socialists, including Sidney and Beatrice Webb, and the free trade unions, all opposed it. Unemployment insurance and related measures were put through in England by such people as Winston Churchill, Lloyd George, Beveridge, Lord Asquith, Hubert Smith, Neville Chamberlain, and Joseph Chamberlain. It is typical of the history of social security that it did not come in on a great wave of popular demand from the mass of people, as Marxians would now like to have us believe. It came largely because of the efforts of farsighted individuals, who were found as often as not among the ranks of those who would be called conservatives.
At the present time I believe that most authorities on this subject consider the United States plan to be the best in operation. Therefore I have chosen to make a few observations concerning our separate systems on a comparative basis. We are aware that the Canadian system in effect is financed on the 3-3-3 formula, with these percentages being collected from sales tax, corporation tax and personal income tax. This formula supplied $603.1 million in the year 1960-61, which represented $10.7 million in excess of receipts over expenditures. In the current year it is estimated that $607 million will be required to finance the necessary payments.
With the flat rate payments of $55 a month I have learned and the minister indicated, that Canadian payments amounted to 2.45 per cent of the national income, whereas in the United States payments amounted to 2.66 per cent of the national income of that country. The difference is accounted for by the fact that in Canada the minimum and maximum are the same, while in the United States the payment ranges from a minimum of $33 to a maximum of $127. There are two very relative points to be borne in mind, namely that the United States per capita income is from 25 per cent to 30 per cent higher than in Canada, and that the United States plan supports a disability and survivors insurance program as well, in addition to the program that we have in effect.
Supply-Health and Welfare
With regard to welfare payments as we understand them, I think the time has come when we must give further consideration to unemployment insurance benefits. This matter has been studied by the authorities in several of the provinces. I am sure hon. members will be aware of this. They have said, and this is also my opinion, that unemployment insurance benefits could be more adequately handled if they were paid out directly by the provinces. As I have said, this has been requested by some of the provinces. In the United States unemployment insurance is handled entirely by the state authorities, and is no concern of the federal government.
In the United States in 1960 the average income for retired workers was $69.50 for a single person and $123.40 for a married person. The differential as compared with the Canadian figures can be discounted, if one chooses to do so, on the basis of the difference in income. One of the great advantages of the United States program, in my thinking, is the benefit paid to widows and their children under the age of 18, or the survivors benefit, and also the disability insurance, which I would advocate, if the government were to institute such a plan. At this point, Mr. Chairman, I think I should say that the United States system is financed by a 3 per cent employee and a 3 per cent employer contribution, with 4J per cent being paid by the self-employed, based on a maximum taxable income of $4,800 for this purpose.
Because of the many experiences I have had where people under the age of 70 have become disabled and are not eligible for old age assistance, I would recommend that the government include the disability class in a prepared program. This I realize, from the experience of 1951, and in consideration of survivors benefits, may create a constitutional problem but I should hope that it would be of minimal proportions. I believe that such a program could be put into effect on a 2 per cent employee and 2 per cent employer basis, and adjusted as experience required. I have been assured that such a program would carry itself financially on a 1 per cent and 1 per cent basis if the 3-3-3 formula were retained; but I would not advocate such a course, because the people want a plan on the basis of contribution so the returns are a personal right as opposed to some of the current thinking. Moreover, I believe the minimum could be raised and the maximum set to allow a flexible scale for those who contribute the maximum, possibly a range from $70 to $100.
Those who have studied this matter will realize that in such a system the problems
7000	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare of portable pensions and of vesting rights would be removed, because there would be a lessening in the tendency to change jobs, which usually results in the employee losing some of these privileges under existing private schemes. Therefore I was interested, of course, in the statement of the Minister of Finance in presenting his budget. Private companies which have expressed certain fears in regard to the implementation of this type of legislation need only to look to the United States, where the experience has been that such insurance sales have increased tremendously since the inception of their program.
I should like to state, Mr. Chairman, that a contributory social security system, as I have referred to it, would foster many of our fundamental beliefs such as self-respect, dignity and personal pride. You may ask why, and my answer is because there would be entitlement by right with no stigma attached, no means test. I believe it is a Christian concern for the state to assist the people of the state, particularly some of the weaker members; for, as Abraham Lincoln stated:
A legitimate function of government is to do for the people what needs to be done, but what they by their individual efforts cannot do quite so well.
Such a plan does not result in the loss or the control of the rights of anyone, nor does it require the sacrifice of any personal freedom. It would be fair to require the participation of all groups in our society. I would not advocate the principle of contracting out such as was done on the inception of the plan in Great Britain.
A flat rate contribution on maximum amounts of income would assure that up to that maximum-and ours might have to be slightly higher than in the United States- the earner in the higher bracket would support the program to a greater degree than the earner whose income is in the lower scale, but to compensate there would also be a graduated scale of benefits which in reality would give the minimum income group more than they could buy for the contribution they actually make, and the maximum less than they would receive on a similar basis.
My observations indicate that beyond doubt this is the general desire of the Canadian people, and I respectfully request consideration of such a program by the minister and the government.

Mr. Chairman, before dealing with the one subject with which I wish to deal at length I should like to make some reference to the remarks made by the hon. member for Timmins. He suggested that, having regard to certain remarks that were made by the first speaker from my party, he could not give credence to any Liberal promises, since such promises had not been fulfilled in the past.
With reference particularly to the provisions respecting hospitalization, which were brought in by the former administration, I suggest that this was one of the most forward looking measures ever introduced. It was introduced by a Liberal majority, and it was designed to be brought into effect only when a majority of Canadians and a majority of the provinces had indicated that they were prepared to accept and pay for such a plan.
The suggestion of the hon. member for Timmins was that the plan should have been imposed from the top whether or not the people of the country were prepared for it. speechtext:
I am not going to deal with all of the matters which come within the minister's purview. As has been said before, this is one of the largest spending of all federal departments. However, I wish to deal with one isolated part of the operations of the department, something which has reference not only to this department but to other departments. Therefore it will be necessary to refer to some of the things which have been done by the Department of Public Works and by the Department of Labour in particular.
I wish to deal specifically with the problems of aging in the community and the contribution which has been made so far by the federal authorities, by voluntary welfare organizations throughout the country and by the provinces. Particularly since the last war this country, in common with most of the other western nations, has been required to pay particular attention to the problems of youth. Because of the population explosion

which took place about the end of the war, because of the fact that we have had a great many young people going through the school system, we have been concerned with using our resources first to give these children public school education on a free basis and then high school education, and in many quarters there is pressure to give them university training.
Only this year we have seen strengthened legislation introduced to deal with the matter of technical training for those who have left the formal education field and require some other training. But too little has been done and too little thought has been given by the public generally to the problems of the aged on the other end of the scale. The aged are not only those who require to be in nursing homes. The aged can be almost any age. Certainly the lowest age which is usually considered to be included is 60, but when one considers related problems, the problems of portability of pensions, the problems of retraining for employment, it is shocking to find that the aged in a modern society are those 40 and over.
These people are increasing in numbers. According to the latest figures I have, which are taken from a report in the Ottawa Citizen of April 18 last of a meeting of the local council of women, the number of those 60 or over in 1921 constituted 7.5 per cent of our population or 660,000 people. By 1951 this had risen to 11.4 per cent or 1,592,000 Canadians, and it is projected that by 1980 the aged group of the Canadian population over 60 will constitute 12.8 per cent or more than 3,400,000 Canadians.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Just before the noon adjournment, I had put certain figures on the record as quoted in a copy of the Ottawa Citizen. Those figures came originally from a study prepared by the research statistics division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, a report of which was issued in June of 1957. Even at that time-and in the past few years the problem has become increasingly important-it was realized that the percentage of the population in Canada above 60 was creating considerably more pressure and would continue to do so. We are reaching a situation in Canada wherein, by reason of the number of years required for young people to take training, whether
Supply-Health and Welfare it be the academic type or the trades training type, it is taking so long for people to become producers in society that, when taken together with those who are forcibly, as a result of pension agreements, employer-employee agreements or the policies of governments, put out to pasture at 60 or 65, there is an increasing burden on the producers of the nation.
If we continue to treat those who are aged, in particular those who are above 60, as individuals who are no longer necessary to the mainstream of society, if we persist in putting them aside, if we persist in saying to them, you cannot stay in this place of employment because other people are coming along and because of your age you are no longer capable of contributing in this employment, then we are going to add to our problems. In addition to this we have the fact that, in the last 60 years, there has been a considerable change in the size of houses now being constructed for the young married people. The young married people are no longer able to keep their aged parents or relatives with them, so this forces the older people out of the home and breaks the family association. The elderly people are thereby cut off from the mainstream society.
Welfare agencies, either govermental or voluntary, are trying to set up recreational programs or "busy" work for the aged. It is my belief from my study of this problem, that the older citizen of Canada does not want to be treated as a special class with particular disabilities. As everyone knows, we all age at a different rate. We all cease to have our full capabilities at a different time. We say that 65 is the time when a Canadian is no longer of any use to his country, is no longer efficient. We make them feel unwanted, that they are no longer useful. It is significant that all studies indicate that there is a higher suicide rate in the group above 60 than in any age group in our nation. These figures are identical with those for the United States. No human being wants to feel he or she is not wanted by the family or the community, to feel there is no purpose in continuing to live. No person wants to be a parasite in society. Everyone wants to be an effective human being and able to contribute all they have throughout their productive period.
Yesterday the hon. member for Leeds referred to the fact that we cannot afford to have trained people in our society who are not contributing to the public welfare. I would suggest that we cannot afford to arbitrarily put people out of work at 65 and dislocate them from everything they have known. We cannot afford the waste of these

Supply-Health and Welfare people. They have the greatest training and the greatest experience. Our philosophers have said that up to age 40 you simply gain experience and beyond 40 you apply it. The problem is one for the nation as well as for the individuals concerned.
In studying this problem, Mr. Chairman, I have written as widely as I could to welfare agencies in both Canada and the United States, and I should like to refer briefly to some of the agencies that are working on some of the problems in relation to the aged. As an indication of the increased interest which is being shown in this particular problem, I may say that in the province of Ontario, with which I am most familiar, there was set up in metropolitan Toronto a social planning council which has been meeting for the past few years dealing with the special problems of the ageing in our community. In addition, the Ontario society of the ageing has been set up and it has called conferences and established study groups. This organization has been responsible for some excellent reports dealing with the problem in Ontario. In 1957, the Ontario society for the ageing called a conference which met for a month in Toronto. A report was published entitled, "Proceedings of First Ontario Conference on Ageing". This conference was attended by individuals from government and from voluntary societies. As I have said, the study lasted for one month at the University of Toronto.
May I, Mr. Chairman, refer to some of the things which were discussed so hon. members will realize the scope of the problem. This is not just a welfare or health problem, but it goes much further than that. These are the subheadings in this report: Mental health in later years; the challenge of the ageing population; financing health services; working together; total community programs; patterns of living of older people in Ontario, and here research was undertaken; the cost of living and retirement income; nutrition for the ageing; pension plans; compulsory retirement plans; the problem of the cost of living; government programs and other sources of income; housing and living arrangements; money available for housing; types of accommodation, including boarding home care and private care; charitable institutions and their contributions; self-contained accommodation; community services; care and rehabilitation at home; friendly visiting; clubs and recreation; educational interests; church and synagogue; senior citizens' service bureau; employment, unemployment and retirement; the effect of the changing patterns of employment; work opportunities; satisfying the psychological needs in retirement; employment of older persons; preretirement counselling and planning; the care,


treatment and rehabilitation of the ageing in hospitals and homes; long term illness in institutions; the acutely ill aged in institutions; private hospitals and nursing homes; the care of the senile aged.
Reference was made to what is being done in the United States and Great Britain. This is a magnificent report and I would commend it to the attention of all hon. members of this committee who are interested in the ageing elements in our population. As a result of this conference subcommittees were set up and after three years' study another one day workshop was set up on March 26, 1960; it was a workshop on ageing. Reports were made as to what had been done in the intervening free period and certain of the research which had been commenced was also reported on. Perhaps one of the most interesting things was of a couple of studies which had been undertaken which indicated that what was necessary in order for an individual who had retired and was living alone to live-just to exist-was between $86 and $90 a month and that for a couple retired, living alone, it would require $130 to $149 a month. This is a modest but adequate living standard and it is only for the province of Ontario. So far as I know that type of study has not been undertaken anywhere else.
In addition to the Ontario society for the ageing there has been magnificent work done by a national board and that is the committee on ageing of the Canadian welfare council of which the Hon. Muriel Fergusson of the other place has the responsibility and honour of being chairman. This agency, which is a well known one, has for the last couple of years been particularly interested in the matter of housing and there have been set up in various provinces particular agencies to deal with housing for the aged.
Most hon. members read the local press here in Ottawa and will have seen that there has been considerable pressure and a considerable number of press reports with respect to a new home for the aged in Ottawa. This is a matter which is becoming increasingly important in all communities across Canada. At one time it was considered sufficient to set up what was called an old people's home, to put there indigent people, to close the door and to forget about them. This is the same sort of thing that once happened in Eskimo societies where you sent the aged out on the ice expecting them never to come back. For too long in Canada we have sent the aged to old people's homes, closed the door, hoped that they would die and that the problem would go away.
In the most recent years we have been considering what can be done not just for

these people but with them, or what can they do for themselves. Certainly the more modern approach appears to be that we do not build an old people's home some place out in the wilds of a community away from all the interrelation of the community, but that we try to build smaller units in down town areas where they can get out, see their friends, go to the theatre and things of this kind.
Housing is only one problem and there has been considerable assistance in the past few years from the Department of Public Works. Under N.H.A. a particular brochure has been prepared called "Housing for Old People". Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have put out this brochure. There are also a great many most interesting booklets which are of assistance to every community which has to face this problem. They include "Housing and Living Arrangements for the Aged", "Everyone Grows Old", "The Needs of the Aged", and things of this kind. They are of assistance and they indicate that some research, study and attention have been given to the problem. But this is fragmentary.
In the Department of Labour a considerable amount of work has been done as well. I have had the benefit from the Department of Labour of a considerable number of booklets indicating the extent of the work they have been doing over the past few years. They have made a study of the older worker as such. They put out in May 1960, in mimeographed form "The Problem of the Older Worker" which is a reference manual containing certain factual information and references to other works. In addition, they have prepared something of particular interest to women, namely a booklet entitled, "A New Career after 30". This is a most interesting study of women above age 30 who launched into new careers and took new training. It indicates that they are a most effective addition to the productive part of the population.
Also in the Department of Labour there has been a considerable program over the last five or six years of a study of pensions-
