speechtext:
Over the last five or six years. Many of these are dated early in 1957. On pension plan and employment of older workers an excellent report has been prepared by the Department of Labour. There was, set up, I believe, in 1953, an interdepartmental committee and there are representatives of labour, of national health and welfare, of veterans affairs, of finance and some other departments who meet to discuss the interrelated problems of ageing. This has been going on now for some eight or nine years and it is producing more and more research information. There is indeed a
Supply-Health and Welfare pamphlet which is put out called "Two Minutes of Employment Facts", pension plans for the employment of older workers. The intent of this was that it should be sent around to employers in order to encourage them to employ people above what would normally be called the pensioning off age.
There were two radio broadcasts made on the older worker problem, the scripts of which are available to the public. There is another booklet called "Speaking Out About the Older Worker Problem" also prepared by the labour department. In addition, there is an excellent study made by Professor S. A. Clark of the University of Toronto on the employability of the older worker. This is a review of his research covering a long period which was produced in October of 1959. It goes into the whole problem in Canada. There are many studies of employing, housing and caring for, in a medical way, older people in the world but not too many Canadian studies.
In addition, the department of health and welfare, since the publication of "The Ageing Worker" by the Department of Labour, has instituted research and has produced a number of pamphlets and pieces of material which have been of assistance to those interested in the problem. There is one booklet produced by this department under date of July, 1959, "Health Services for Public Assistance Recipients in Canada" with particular reference to older people and "Rehabilitation Services in Canada", part 2, which sets out the provincial and local programs available. This is under date of February, 1959.
In addition, there have been a number of private or semi-private groups most Interested in the ageing. I would particularly refer hon. members to the problem which is clearly set out in the Saturday Review of January 28, 1961, which deals in particular with the desperate world of the senior citizen in the United States. Apart from the figures which are given there the problem is identical to that in Canada. I would commend this to all hon. members.
In addition, through its leaflet "Occupational Health Review" volume 12, No. 2, 1960, this department has put out a long and informative article on the lengthening life span which again gives evidence of the increasing numbers as well as the increasing percentages of the aged in our community. This is something which we can no longer allow to be attacked on a piecemeal basis. In the United States, as a result of the type of pressure that there has been from private agencies over the past two years, there was

Supply-Health and Welfare held on January 9 to 12, of 1961, at Washington the first White House conference on ageing. It may be of interest to hon. members to know that there were about 2,800 voting delegates attending that conference and there were 20 Canadians there as invited observers. Papers were produced as a result of the conference which dealt with all aspects of ageing. In the field of federal-state, such as our federal-provincial programs of public assistance, surveys and studies were considered that had been undertaken by research organizations and universities without knowing that anyone else was undertaking the same type of work. This conference dealt with the increasing concern in the fields of health, rehabilitation, housing, income maintenance, and education and retraining of the aged.
The population trends on the North American continent are inescapable. Because of the triumph of medicine over those diseases which have caused our people to die at early ages we have an increasingly larger group of the ageing in our communities. It is necessary that they be treated as human beings; it is necessary that they continue to be a part of our population. Most individuals who are of retirement age do not like to be called senior citizens, aged or ageing. I think all of us would like to say that we are forever young. However, when one realizes that because of the present lack of portability of pensions even 40 year olds, or in some cases those in their thirties, fall into the classification of the aged. They cannot move from one place to another because of the lack of portability of pensions, and because of the pressures of modern living their bodies age more quickly than they did in the past and people are falling within the classifications of the ageing well below the age of 60 or 65 years.
Mr. Chairman, most of the work which has been done by various departments of this government was instituted prior to 1957, as anyone who would study these publications will readily ascertain, because one can see from the length of time devoted to the studies and the date the reports were produced that is was a Liberal administration which brought in all the social welfare legislation which is on the statute books of this country. These were the studies which were undertaken and I would venture to guess that had that administration continued in office, at this point we would have a co-ordinating agency to devote concentrated attention to this particular problem.
Hon. members will have noticed within the past few months discussions in the Financial Post, in the local press and the national press respecting the Canadian welfare council meeting which was held recently, where the director of the council, Mr. Kenneth Parker,
[Miss LaMarsh.l
pointed out in his presidential report that "better welfare is not achieved only at the cost of a higher total of public spending".
Notwithstanding the fact that these people are leaders in bringing together health workers and social workers in a community, they said that the total cost of Canada's public health and welfare programs, in the vicinity of $3 billion including taxes and private donations from volunteer agencies, was not enough; that it was necessary for a searching study to be made in Canada of the whole approach of social welfare measures, and particularly of those involving the aging. There was an editorial to this effect, which hon. members may have seen, in the Ottawa Citizen of June 1, 1961.
In March of this year the Financial Post undertook a thorough study of whether or not in Canada we are receiving enough for our welfare dollar. It was indicated that 11.4 per cent of our national income is devoted to welfare payments and that this is steadily increasing each year, but that there is a considerable amount of duplication in private and government agencies. Reference was also made in the Financial Post of February 18, 1961 to a tremendous new study which has been undertaken in the province of Ontario under the provincial department of labour. This is a study of Canadians over the age of 45 years in which from 1958, 2,000 men in the province are being studied until they reach age 65. This is perhaps the first such study undertaken anywhere in a western democracy. This study will provide invaluable information, but the information will only be relevant to the province of Ontario. It is not sufficient, I would suggest, to leave this to the provincial departments, because it is a national problem.
There is no question that, like education, the administration of assistance to the ageing can best be done on a local level and on a level in which they themselves can actively participate. I would suggest that, following the report of the 20 observers who attended the White House conference on the ageing, following the report of the Canadian welfare council, a massing together of the information which has been brought together in the various departments of government and the interdepartmental committee, from private welfare agencies, and from provincial departments, now is the time for this department to take a bold step and to call a national conference on the ageing in which there will be participation not only by federal-provincial departments, not only by those whose whole responsibility is to assist in the problems of the ageing, but also by all volunteer agencies. The Canadian Red Cross has been active for years in matters

respecting the ageing, and the Canadian welfare council, as I said before, has a particularly active group set up to deal principally with the problems of the ageing.
Mr. Chairman, may I in closing refer to an article which appeared in the February 1961 issue of the magazine Health, published for the Canadian family by the Health League of Canada. The article is by Dr. Edward L. Bortz and is entitled:
Breaking those "ageing" barriers.
On page 19 of the magazine he writes:
Then another problem, perhaps the greatest problem facing society today, appears, namely, what to do with all the old folk. Surely we do not want a majority of our population to be tottery, senile, vegetating parasites. Would it not seem that experience and maturity that come as we grow older should have some social usefulness that we have not yet identified? Too often we invite premature decay by withdrawing from the active stream of social usefulness and sit on the sidelines. The zest and joy of living are likely to be lost if one withdraws from productive living. One becomes a consumer instead of a producer, and the world already has too many consumers. The yardstick of social value, so far as the individual is concerned, is just that easy to apply.
It is necessary, then, Mr. Chairman, for the good not only of those involved, those who are ageing, but for the good of our country nationally that we now bring together the information which has been obtained at all levels and undertake research and study in order that those in our community who have the greatest experience, the greatest judgment, shall be able to continue to contribute to the mainstream of our community life.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before presenting my remarks may I extend my congratulations to the minister, who I understand is celebrating his birthday today. It is not very often that a minister has the privilege of celebrating his birthday and also presenting his estimates on the same day. I am sure we all wish him well in his future health and welfare. May I say to the minister:
Count not your age by years you live But by the happiness you give,
The friends you make, the good you do,
The confidence that's placed in you,
The little things that day by day,
Bring cheer to others on life's way,
And count this day one more mile,
Upon the road to God and things worth while.
I appreciate the opportunity of speaking briefly on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. This department, under the energetic supervision of the minister and his staff, is no doubt one of the most important in the administration of our country's affairs, and the fine advances made in social justice are proof of the competent work being done by all those concerned.
I understand that assistance to every category of social justice

old age security, old
Supply-Health and Welfare age assistance, blind and disability allowance, unemployment assistance, not too well known to some Canadians, hospital insurance and health grants-has been substantially increased. Perhaps one of the most beneficial improvements was the lowering from 20 to 10 years of the residence requirement in regard to old age pensions. As we know, recipients are now permitted to take their pension with them when leaving Canada on a permanent basis. Senior citizens living outside of Canada, and those contemplating doing so, are very appreciative of this legislation. Many of these recipients living in Canada, happy and satisfied with conditions here, are obliged to leave our country for health reasons or because of family ties and uncontrollable circumstances.
Mr. Chairman, about a year ago I spoke in this house in favour of the new federal plans concerning emergency measures and civil defence. At this time I should like to add that the progress and development that have taken place since that time have justified the optimism I expressed then as to the workability of the new plan. It has been brought to my attention that the Department of National Health and Welfare has assumed two important responsibilities; first, the arrangements for the maintenance of public health and welfare in case of disaster. This is in accordance with government planning for wartime emergency. Two departmental divisions, the emergency health division and the emergency welfare services division, are continuously planning and preparing for this task. The emergency health services staffed by experts in the health field have in operation an $18 million medical stockpiling program. This supplies to the purchasing, packaging and distribution and storage depots across Canada, tremendous amounts of first aid supplies, medicines, drugs and surgical equipment. Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of our discussion of the Department of National Health and Welfare estimates to deal with a subject very close to my heart, the matter of improving the lot of the epileptics with regard to medical care, research and the relation of this disease to everyday life.
Of all diseases affecting human beings, none has been less understood than epilepsy. In fact, people still have all sorts of antiquated notions about it, even though medical science

offers good hopes of recovery, because it is a known fact that nowadays 50 per cent of cases can be successfully treated.
The purpose of my remarks today is to help put an end to those antiquated ideas about epilepsy and to that lack of understanding which amounts to a lack of charity. I do not know whether we have very accurate statistics on the number of such cases, but I am informed from a reliable source that there are 10,500 epileptics in the Montreal area, 40,000 in the province of Quebec and around 145,000 in Canada.
People who suffer from that disease must fight on two fronts: first, the disease itself and, then, society whose lack of understanding gives rise to all kinds of complexes among epileptics, society which does not give these people the moral and economic support they need to put up an efficient fight under normal conditions.
It is said that the term "epilepsy" derives from a Greek word meaning "seizure"; apparently, that disease goes back to the remotest history of mankind. It seems that those seizures or fits, which vary in seriousness and frequency from one individual to another, are brought about by some irritation of the brain the causes of which are mostly unknown to this day. Epilepsy is not an hereditary disease as such, since it is said that only one epileptic out of every 50 has an epileptic child. In some cases, an operation is necessary but in most cases drugs are the recommended treatment. As I said, the purpose of these remarks is to get both the government and the public to show more understanding for the plight of epileptics and take positive steps to help them.
May I suggest three types of measures already within our reach. First, in the research field, I think we should promote and speed up medical research in order to develop the most appropriate drugs for this disease. "We should keep abreast of developments in medical research, not only in the western countries but also in the countries behind the iron curtain, because in the field of research there is no such thing as frontiers. The officials in the Department of National Health and Welfare should be given every facility to take an active part in any medical conference, anywhere through the world, in order to be always on the watch for any new treatment.
I would be very much in favour of the federal and provincial governments joining in a construction program for various research centres in Canada's major cities, where thousands of epileptics could be admitted, so that we could give them the appropriate
Supply-Health and Welfare care and promote their rehabilitation to a normal life, without their having to depend on anyone.
As a second step, I would suggest that epileptic children of school age attend regular schools.
At this point I must say something which is probably not known to any hon. member. If a six, seven or eight year old child, is registered in a school in the province of Quebec and the school authorities notice that he or she suffers from epilepsy, this child is sent home. Epileptics are not getting any education, whereas they need the benefit of education more than others. Such conditions are unwarranted, indeed. Experience has shown that most epileptics who have had a chance of getting some education, and more particularly those whose parents were able to afford private tuition-and this is the only way they can be educated-have always got on in the struggle for life, and never became a burden for the state.
If the only result of my remarks were to rouse the public conscience with regard to that extraordinary fact that epileptic children have no possibility of education, that they are not admitted in our schools, I think I shall not have wasted my time in drawing public attention to a problem for which an eventual solution may be found.
I have a third suggestion to submit. It deals with the adult epileptic, who had no chance of getting an education. How can such an individual, who, in spite of his illness, is able to take on a responsible job in many fields have a chance of being employed? Unfortunately, we are living in a callous society, which is often lacking in charity. I must say that we are not very progressive in this field, as I am informed that in Great Britain for instance, there are laws providing that in large companies, 2 or 3 per cent of the labour force must be made up of handicapped people such as epileptics. I wonder why we could not do the same thing here. If we want industry to do its share, if we want our industries to give epileptics an opportunity to work, it is only fair that the state should set the example.
I was saying a moment ago that generally speaking our society is callous. However, Canadians are also very generous people, and when face squarely with a problem of this kind, I am sure they will respond and give jobs to those handicapped, who seek nothing more.
Moreover, if the government were to set aside 1 or 2 per cent of the jobs available in the federal civil service for those people, this would provide employment for 300 to 400 of

Supply-Health and Welfare them. We must not forget that nothing prevents an epileptic from marrying and raising a family.
I also stated a moment ago that this disease is not hereditary. I hope the minister will give special consideration to this suggestion and will be able to prevail upon the government to lead the way in this field.
In closing, may I say a few words about two organizations which have been showing great devotion in the care of those sick people. I refer particularly to the Dieppe home, at St. Hilaire, an establishment devoted to the treatment and rehabilitation of male epileptics. Unfortunately, when those people are released from the Dieppe home, there are no jobs available to them, despite the fact that they are able to work.
Moreover, there is no institution to take care of women thus afflicted. They have to depend upon public charity or their relatives. So far, the government has not taken any real step to assist that rather large number of our fellow citizens.
I was saying a moment ago that we have in Canada 145,000 epileptics who expect us to come to their assistance. They are not asking for favours, but only the support they are entitled to. All they want is to be able to play a productive part in our society.
I hope that the minister will give serious consideration to my suggestions.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the Department of National Health and Welfare is one department that touches practically every home and every individual in the country in some way, shape or form during their lifetime, and today I want to extend the thanks of the citizens of Brantford for the very generous help we have had in building two new hospitals. We are fortunate that we have two practically brand new hospitals, one operated by the sisters of St. Joseph who do a very excellent job and operate the hospital most efficiently, and the other our own Brantford General hospital, a 500 bed hospital. Incidentally, I happen to have the honour of being a member of the board of governors of this big institution.
One point that I want to bring before the government today has to do with the building of nurses' homes and nurses' training schools. We are in the process now of trying to draw up plans and raise the money to build a new nurses' home and a new nurses' training school. This is a big problem because in a large hospital such as ours we need from 60 to 75 girls going into training for nursing every year. This means that we have to have a building to look after at least 225 girls because we must have enough beds for the trainees and also for those engaged in supervisory duties.
This is a big responsibility for the municipality. Because of the way hospital grants are now made and because of the fact that people coming under the Ontario hospital plan can enter any hospital, when the municipality is called upon to construct these large buildings in order to maintain these hospitals it puts a terrific burden on the taxpayer who is already suffering a good deal from high taxes in municipalities throughout the country.
Some time ago when the government extended to 75 per cent the subsidy to vocational training schools in order to help to train the male population of our country, I asked myself why a subsidy of the same proportions was not also extended to training schools for nurses. After all, if we do not train nurses we will not have the necessary staff for our hospitals. New hospitals with

plenty of beds are of little value unless we have efficient nurses and can get girls to enter training as nurses in order to staff these hospitals.
This is a problem that every hospital faces right throughout Ontario and I suppose right throughout the country. We have brought nurses from overseas but they did not stay too long. While they helped to tide us over a period when we were very short of trained nurses, we have to rely on the nurses we can train in our own hospitals to maintain them and to look after the patients there. The building we now have for a nurses' home is not adequate by any means. The fire department would like to condemn it and not have it used at all but we must continue to use it until such time as we can construct a new building.
Other hospitals have a slight advantage over us when they can show prospective trainees a new nurses' home and an excellent training school. We have very excellent teachers in our hospital and that counteracts to some extent the difficulty we are having. Not too long ago the government saw fit to help parents with children going to university and if parents of university children can be helped in some way I certainly think that parents with daughters training for nurses should also be given some assistance. As you know, the trainees receive practically no remuneration for the first two years of their training, and I think their parents certainly should be given some consideration so far as income tax is concerned in order to help keep the girls we have and induce girls to train as nurses.
We have heard a good deal today from various hon. members about our old people, our senior citizens. I hope that before too long we will be able to increase the assistance to our older people. I am happy that I was a supporter of the government in 1957 when it raised the old age assistance pension to a level that enabled these people to at least live in some degree of comfort rather than only exist as had been the case before. When we hear about social legislation being brought in, it is important to remember that it is of little or no use unless it is made good enough so that people have to live on and are not existing from hand to mouth and having to go to welfare agencies in order to get enough to sustain themselves. The people who are now reaching the age when they will receive old age pensions are people who went through the last depression. As one who is old enough to have had that experience, I can say that I know what it was to go through the thirties. These people lost everything through no fault of their own. Then the war came and the depression ended-that was the only thing that did end it. When the economy
Supply-Health and Welfare slowed down again, these people were the first to be laid off because they were in the age categories which the factories wanted to eliminate in terms of employment. These are the people who need this extra assistance in order to get the necessities of life. In a country such as ours, these older people should not have to go to welfare agencies with their hat in their hands to ask for enough in order to live.

We in Brantford have the problems of the blind brought to our attention more forcibly than other people because we have the Ontario school for the blind in our city. Pupils come from all over Canada. When one visits this school, one is amazed to see how these youngsters are trained to participate in all types of sports as well as the different vocations for which they are suited in order to enable them to earn a livelihood. However, there are always some who cannot be trained, and some senior adults who need extra help. I would commend to the minister the brief presented by the Canadian institute for the blind and urge him to give help to the older blind people. We have a man in Brantford who looks after the needs of the blind. He is blind himself. I refer to Mr. Ian Grills. He does an amazing job in finding occupations for these older people and helping them work out a new way of life. He certainly should be commended for the excellent work he has done.

The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence says, "Hear, hear". I am afraid his enthusiasm has outrun his knowledge. Let me say this. I happened to mention that they did pass some considerable body of legislation after it was advocated for many years by the Liberals and the Labour party in Great Britain. The credit for the first old age security or pension legislation must go, without a doubt, to the Liberal party in Great Britain. I have a volume of United Kingdom Hansard on my desk because I just wondered if my memory was slipping by reason of increasing age. Here I find a speech by a member of the Conservative party in which he says frankly they must give credit to the Liberal government, which was the government of Campbell Bannerman's day, and later, for the introduction of the old age pension legislation. I thought I would mention that because I think it is wise for us to keep our facts straight. I give the Conservatives of Great Britain great credit for allowing themselves to be influenced by the members of the Liberal and Labour parties of the day. I give Winston Churchill, the former prime minister of Great Britain, great credit because of his natural common sense. But let us not forget this fact. When former prime minister Winston Churchill first advocated old age pensions he was a member of the Liberal party in Great Britain. But later on,-he was a very common sense prime minister-he saw the need for this provision and his government moved forward in that direction.
Generally speaking we in this country are far behind Great Britain and European countries with respect to over-all social welfare legislation. I suppose it comes from our more recent pioneer circumstances in the first instance and second because we are not a unitary state. I admit that it is much more difficult to develop an over-all security program in a country such as Canada in which there is a federal government and ten provincial governments that have to be considered and their wishes with respect to policy, administration and finance, shall I say, obtained and agreement reached.
In this country there is a need, as there has been for years, for an over-all security program. If there is any question about the need for it and about the thinking in this

direction, I just wish to refer to a very interesting conversation with the former chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. Butler. I was ribbing him a bit. It was shortly after the Conservative government came into power in 1951. I said to him, "Mr. Butler, in view of the history of your party since 1895 with respect to over-all security programs, what are you going to do now that you are in power?" Do you know what he said to me? He said, "An over-all security program is a necessity in the modern age. It is demanded by the British people. It is serving a great purpose. It meets a great need so far as the British people are concerned. As far as our government is concerned I will tell you this. Our policy as a Conservative government is to continue to improve the revolution." That is because there is a great change in thinking as a result of changing circumstances. There is the advocacy of these things for almost a generation when they were unpopular but finally the will of the people prevails and governments in a democracy are obliged to reflect that will.
While an over-all security program is necessary, the foundations must be laid by the state, shall I say, so there is a minimum security with respect to health, employment, old age and so on. I do not overlook the necessity under the best arrangements for a continued operation of private agencies. In my opinion there will always be a place for compassion and personal responsibility and efforts in this respect. Regardless of the type of society we have, we must have an opportunity for those sentiments to find expression through organized groups and through the efforts of individuals as further supplements to anything that the state can do.
What about the need in this country? I was just looking at this copy of Canadian Welfare magazine which is published monthly. I think it is the latest edition. In this magazine there is a very interesting article written by Mr. E. F. Watson and entitled "How Much is Enough in Social Assistance". I wish to quote one paragraph in order to indicate the circumstances that exist in Canada. I am not quoting this material on a partisan basis but rather to indicate the opinion of a very experienced person in this field. The first paragraph of this article reads as follows:
Hunger and grinding poverty continue to exist for too many people in Canadian communities today.
In 1961 there are still men, women and children who are not getting enough to eat, who are living in appalling housing and who lack sufficient clothing to keep them warm. Unprecedented national productivity, rising wage levels and vastly Increased social welfare expenditures have left this segment of the population in an economic and social backwash.
Supply-Health and Welfare
I think that is quite true and that it is one of the anomalies of our present civilization.
Before going on to say a few words about an over-all security program I wish to refer to the annual report of the executive director of the Canadian welfare council with regard to the part that is still played by private agencies. I mention this matter because I am a great believer in individuals accepting some responsibility within the field of their circumstances and so on. I read in this report an interesting paragraph:
Another thing we observe as we look around is the vigorous growth everywhere evident in the voluntary welfare field. Throughout the whole country many forms of health service, child and family welfare, recreation programs, programs for delinquent youth and the aftercare of adult offenders, housing for the aged and a large variety of other facilities and services continue to be provided largely under private auspices, although in a number of instances with financial subsidies from public funds.
A notable feature of the private welfare movement in Canada during recent years, and one of the secrets of its present strength, is the development of federated financing through community funds. Today there are 107 such funds across the country as contrasted with 54 just a decade ago. During the same period the Canadian per capita contribution to community funds has increased by 50 per cent to well over $3, the number of agencies receiving support has more than doubled to around 1,800 and the total money raised, now approaching thirty million dollars annually, has nearly tripled. This growth during the 50's is by any standard impressive, and greatly exceeds that of the entire earlier period back to 1917 when the first Canadian federation was established in Montreal.
I will tell you what I think that indicates. I think it indicates that when governments take a lead and give effect to policies, as the federal government has done in certain fields in the administration of this department, it is a spur to action on the part of private organizations and agencies and even to individuals. I say again that whatever the state does-and the state must accept its full responsibility-there is a great deal of scope for compassion exercised through private agencies and through the activities of individuals.
In 1958 the Canadian welfare council adopted a policy statement for social security for Canada. I wish to refer to it briefly because it is still up to date. This statement was the result of a considerable study by very well informed and experienced persons in this field, and I understand that these recommendations were presented to the federal government at that time. What do they say here? I am going to quote just some of them. While there are some things that we could not agree with entirely, possibly where they do not go far enough in some instances, I think the general outlook is excellent and progressive.

Mr. Chairman, I heard a sort of bellow over to my left. I did not know whether it was complimentary or otherwise. Oh, I understand. I had thought the hon. gentleman was going to rise in order to make some comment on what I was saying. It is the pipe line section of the chamber. I read as follows:
Recommendation 1:
The present universal flat rate pension commencing at age 70 should be retained.
That is in view of the proposal being put forward for an over-all security program. I think that is quite correct, and we believe that is correct until it is replaced by some over-all security plan which provides for something better.
Recommendation 2:
Consideration should be given to arrangements which would enable certain classes of people in the 65-69 age group to qualify for the old age security pension.
I have received a number of letters on that question and a number of instances have been brought to my attention which indicate that the government should give immediate consideration to that recommendation because of the circumstances in which people between 65 and 69 years of age find themselves at the present time. I continue:
Recommendation 3:
Provision should be made for a continuing review and periodic consideration of adjustment in the amount of the universal flat rate pension on the basis of adequate statistical data relating to such important factors as minimum needs and levels of expenditure of older people.
I am sure all hon. members of the committee have during recent months received letters from organizations representing old age security recipients and old age pensioners' organizations urging reconsideration and adjustment of the present basic rate of pension because of the increase in the cost of living since the pension was raised in 1957. We have given consideration, and properly so, to disability war pensioners; we have given consideration to recipients of war veterans allowance, and I think it is now appropriate for us to recognize the needs of those on old age security and old age assistance. Recommendation 4:
Financial assistance should be made available by the provinces to all persons 65 and over who are in need, with federal sharing of benefit costs.
This recommendation encompasses assistance to two groups of persons in particular, recipients of the universal old age security pension who are in need, and persons 65 to 69 years of age who are in need. I know this is not as simple a problem as appears on the surface, but I trust that in the very near future we will hear of a conference being

called among the federal government, provincial governments and private agencies to discuss the problem faced today by the aged in Canada. At this stage I wish to compliment the hon. member for Niagara Falls on what I thought was a very logical speech. It showed good preparation coupled with, as usual, excellent presentation. I continue:
Recommendation 5:
A joint parliamentary committee should be established to study the question of contributory wage-related old age benefits in addition to the universal pension and to make recommendations to parliament.
When the minister replies to the various questions raised on item No. 1 I hope he will inform the committee whether the government has given consideration to that recommendation. I continue:
Recommendation 6:
Whether or not a compulsory contributory old age pension program is developed, the dominion government should lay down appropriate standards for private pension plans in connection with which income tax deductions are granted.
At this stage I certainly want to support the remarks of the hon. member for Timmins, who urged the government to make provision, in co-operation with the provinces, for a national portable or transferable pension scheme which would cover all persons in Canada. There is responsibility on the federal government because this question is directly related to exemptions from income tax and the action of the federal government will largely determine the benefits and the type of legislation which will be put into operation by the provinces. The leadership in this field must come from the federal government if the provinces are going to provide any satisfactory type of transferable or portable pension. The next recommendation reads as follows:
Recommendation 7:
There should be a federal public assistance act which would be, in effect, an extension of the Unemployment Assistance Act-
Then it spells out the details. I do think there is great need for further consideration of that problem in view of the present liabilities and costs thrown upon municipalities. That is a rather involved and complicated question, and I certainly support the recommendation of the council. Recommendation No. 8 reads:
The operation of all public assistance programs should be based upon sound and clearly defined standards, particularly with respect to:
a. Amount of assistance.
i.	A definition of what constitutes a minimum level of health and decency.
ii.	A schedule of minimum requrements based upon this definition, and related to the age and size of the family unit.

iii.	The periodic translation of minimum requirements into monetary terms, appropriate to the specific community, which would form the basis of public assistance payments.
I think that is very necessary indeed. I have read statistical tables dealing with the minimum requirements, for example in Toronto and in some other places in Canada. No standard has been set which can be taken as a yardstick across this country as to what minimum requirements are necessary.
In connection with unemployment insurance the council makes several recommendations, but as those do not come under this department I shall not mention them. The council concludes with a recommendation for intergovernmental co-operation and administrative standards. I think that is very necessary indeed. There is a great diversity of standards between the federal government and the provinces with respect to administrative practices and, shall I say, uniformity of administration and procedure.
I think something could be done in this connection along the lines of the uniformity of legislation committee which meets once every year. I understand the Solicitor General, the Minister of Justice and the attorneys general of the provinces, or their representatives, meet once a year in order to maintain uniformity of legislation. I think this could be the basis of an excellent study. I think this is the sort of problem to which the other place, having more leisure and freed from day to day, shall I say, partisan strife and things of that sort, could devote some attention after the fashion of their present land use study and the excellent study that has been made with respect to manpower and employment.
This is the type of study that takes time in order to assimilate the information with respect to procedures in other countries and Canada and, on the basis of that information, devise a standard of administration and procedure which is accepted from the Atlantic to the Pacific and will provide greater efficiency, lower costs in relation to the units served and therefore more service to the Canadian people from the tax money expended. Recommendation 19 reads as follows:
The dominion government should make funds available for demonstration and research projects, in the causes and prevention of dependency, social and economic rehabilitation, and similar problems.
That was mentioned, Mr. Chairman, by previous speakers and it has validity. This would take some time, possibly years, to accomplish but it should be given consideration. Recommendation No. 20:
Machinery should be devised to ensure regular communication among provinces, and between provinces and the dominion government, on all welfare matters of common interest.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I do not know whether there have been any changes in the channels of communication since these recommendations were presented to the government, but I presume that as years go by they are improving. I remember that when the old age pensions act was first introduced, I think it was in 1926, dealing with the problem in British Columbia, in conversation with officials we were faced with the atmosphere-this is the impression I obtained-dealing at arms length, as it were, with the senior government. However, I think that situation has greatly improved over the years. Recommendation No. 21 provides:
The dominion government should establish a broadly representative body of competent persons, the purpose of which would be to keep under constant review all aspects of Canada's social security program and to advise on changes and improvements that may from time to time be desirable.
That is in general terms a very worth-while recommendation. I am not sure just how it can be given effect, but possibly it could be accomplished by including it on the agenda of the type of conference mentioned by the hon. member for Niagara Falls. I think it should be given serious consideration.
The final recommendation is:
The dominion government should appoint a royal commission to study all aspects of social security for which it has a direct or indirect responsibility and more particularly to make recommendations with respect to-
The present royal commission I understand will not be as comprehensive as that provided for in the recommendation of the council.
We are living in a changing society in which we are depending more upon industry than agriculture. This creates many problems which did not exist 40 or 50 years ago. We cannot remain stagnant. First of all we must try to catch up with those who are ahead of us in the United Kingdom and Europe, but we have some way to go before accomplishing that.
I am not suggesting for one moment that these problems are to be solved easily or overnight, but I think the recommendations of the council should be seriously considered by the government and by the members of this committee because they come from a body with a long history of experience in this field.
I know the minister has great respect for the work being done in Canada at this time by similar agencies on national and provincial levels, but we in this group have the feeling that we have not, to date, laid the broad foundations upon which to build the very necessary and comprehensive over-all social security program which Canadian people need and which Canada can well afford.

Supply-Health and Welfare
A few minutes ago I was looking at the report in respect to the problem of social security for aged people in United States and Canada submitted by Dr. Robert M. Clark, which was tabled in the house on March 5, 1959. So far that report has been apparently a matter of academic interest, as far as the government is concerned. Possibly the minister can give us further information as to what the government intends to do in respect to those proposals which can be related to the information contained in this report. I suggest this report indicates how slowly we are moving in this field.
As years go by the need increases, but the government has not, from our point of view, laid the broad foundations necessary to erect the structure of over-all security. Leadership must come from the federal government in this field first of all, although there is a great deal of work done by provincial governments and private agencies, because it is the central government and has the facilities as well as the opportunity of providing the financial assistance required. That leadership must be followed by co-operation between this government and the provincial governments. They must first reach an agreement on the basis of an over-all security program. There are some very good portions of this in effect now, but agreement must be reached in respect to the financing of this program, as well as agreement regarding its administration.
I am confident that if the Canadian people were presented with such a program and told of the cost they would accept it. We do not get something for nothing, but only that which we are willing to pay for, whether it is from corporations or individuals, because two and two make four under a capitalist or socialist administration. I am sure that if the government laid the groundwork for an over-all security program and presented it to the provinces and the people, informing them of its cost and the taxation necessary to carry it forward, it would be acceptable. We in this group do not suggest that we can get something for nothing, but I am sure Canadians would welcome such a forward step which should have been taken years ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should first like to wish the minister a happy birthday. I am sure he can hear me although he has just left his seat. I hope he will have many more as minister of this department. I should also like to congratulate him for the splendid job he has done as well as for the capable and efficient manner in which he is administering his department.
Perhaps I might just mention a few of the things which were badly needed that he has provided. They are; the doubling of grants in respect to hospital beds, the implementation of hospital insurance as well as the various other building grants to hospitals for internes' quarters, nurses' residences, and so forth. Those are only a very few of the legislative measures which have been brought forward since this minister took charge of this department.
I am sure that I do not need to remind him that he also heads the department which spends 22 cents of every dollar that is spent by this government, and in that regard is second only to the Department of National Defence which spends 26 cents of each dollar spent. I am sure that if we look ahead we will find it is only a matter of years until the Department of National Health and Welfare becomes the largest spending department in the federal government.
As one looks ahead and realizes that more and more hospital beds will be required as the span of life is increased one will understand that special emphasis must be placed on the provision of hospital accommodation for elderly people who are chronically ill. Surely those individuals will not require the expensive equipment and buildings necessary for the treatment of active and acutely ill patients for whom we must construct hospitals at a cost of $12,000 to $15,000 per bed. I suggest accommodation could be built for the chronically ill at approximately half that cost.
It is my contention that chronically ill elderly citizens are the responsibility of governments. Many of these people find it difficult today to find accommodation unless they

live in areas where nursing homes have been certified. Those certified homes receive $5 per day per patient from the commission. In comparison, I suggest that the average cost per active permanent hospital bed in Canada is over $18 per day, or almost four times the cost of treatment and accommodation for chronically ill individuals. This certainly applies in Ontario. I also wonder how many active patient hospital beds are being used at this high rate of chronically ill individuals who could be looked after in nursing homes. In this connection I should like to deal in a few moments with mental health. While I appreciate that this is the responsibility of provincial governments, I wonder whether more research could not be done at the federal level. I am aware that Dr. Farquharson has pointed out the scarcity of personnel to carry on this work, but I am also aware of the old proverb that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
I am going to speak for a few moments on the mental health of our people because I believe, with the stresses and strains we are now subjected to, more and more of our people suffer emotional upsets. In this regard I think we should take a look at this very important problem when we realize that one out of 10 babies born in Canada will wind up in a mental institution; that mental and senile deterioration will increase as our life span lengthens. In the last 60 years it has lengthened 20 years. The fact is that one out of every 10 people is either mentally imbalanced or has a serious problem in adjusting himself. It is estimated that 2 per cent of our population is substandard in intelligence. It is stated that 15 per cent of all our school children and university students need psychiatric counsel and it is a well known fact that 2 per cent of our population are alcoholics and need treatment at various times in hospitals or in mental institutions. Indeed, Dr. Wolf states that 50 per cent of all hospital patients suffer from emotional problems that delay their recovery and their stay in hospital was, according to his figures, three times as long as in the normal case. Thus this has increased greatly our hospital costs of which this government pays one-third.
This makes us wonder whether progress is active enough in the research field including researh on virus infection; whether enough dollars are being spent to explore all avenues. Virus sickness, including the common cold, can cost this nation a vast sum in terms of research, treatment and the loss of time of employees from work. Polio is being conquered. The success in this field is a great tribute to the work being done both by the federal and provincial governments; but, what 90205-6-443*
Supply-Health and Welfare about some of the other viruses? What about the virus of measles, for instance, that works on the pregnant mother with the end result a defective child may be born? Should all pregnant women who are not immunized be given measles serum? Should pamphlets be put out by the federal government advising that this should be done?
The province of Ontario has a very fine health department. It has a very capable administrator in the person of Dr. Mat. Dymond. Duplication is costly and unnecessary. Let us make sure that we cover the field properly by aiding and helping the provinces in the fields in which they are unable to undertake and incapable of undertaking the necessary research.
What about the welfare of our older people? More and more are living beyond the arbitrary years. The hon. member for Niagara Falls mentioned the importance of our senior citizens. This is indeed a problem. Just as an illustration, there are more than 5,000 people in the United States who are over 100 years old. This is an astounding figure. It just illustrates that more and more people are entering into the geriatric field. Indeed, in the province of Ontario they organized a geriatric section in the Ontario Medical Association. I believe about two months ago they had their annual meeting in the city of Toronto. Our arbitrary retirement age was set at the time of Bismarck, and that is getting close to 100 years ago. It is ridiculous for us today to be following the same premise. At the time of Bismarck, the average person lived to be 40 years of age; today he lives to be 70 years. We have to take another look at this question.
A great many of these older people live in their own homes, but they are unable to carry on normal household duties to the full extent that they should. The husband and wife are living there. In many instances, if a well cooked meal was prepared and taken to them they could continue living at home. That is being done in some parts of the United States; they call it "meals on wheels". Those people get one good cooked meal a day and they stay in their homes where they are happy in their own environment, without the cost of housing them, thus saving the government millions of dollars. The same thing applies to cleaning up and looking after the house. If a welfare worker were to go in the home once a week and probably do some of the heavier work the old people could carry on. The premises would be kept clean and the old people would be cheered up by the welfare worker. I would suggest to the federal government that they give leadership to the

Supply-Health and Welfare provincial governments in some of those things that have been pointed out, particularly by the United States geriatric society.
We always speak about the pensioners and the increases needed in their pensions. I believe in this. I am in favour of increases but also let me say that I have seen old people die not for want of money but for want of love. Love and the feeling of being wanted are very necessary if we are to have a successful program for the aged. As a matter of fact, this is fundamental. Again this is something that should be instituted at the community level. It costs nothing. Let us put it into practice.
I want to touch on another problem which concerns our children. I hope I am not making too many suggestions to the minister because I know some of the problems he has. I believe that the federal government should assist in or carry out a plan across Canada to supply milk to all the school children. This is done in nearly every country today that has a standard of living comparable with ours. Canada is particularly fortunate in having some of the finest dairy cows in the world. Why we should be behind other countries in this field is very difficult to understand. No better food could be provided for a growing child at such a low cost.
I want to say a few words about cardiovascular diseases which are caused by a high cholesterol diet. The villain is said to be cream, butter, animal fats, all products produced in abundance in our northern climate. Not only are they important to our economy but milk and cheese are cheap sources of protein, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin A. It has been contended that butter, cream and fat in the meal would cause heart disease, particularly coronary thrombosis. People have been urged to use less fat, to discontinue butter and cream and to drink skim milk or powdered skim milk instead of whole milk.
I believe it is readily admitted today that humans obtain their cholesterol in one of three ways: first, by eating foods that contain it; second, by manufacturing it from the starch, sugar and protein they consume; third, by manufacturing cholesterol within the body which varies in reverse with the amount of cholesterol they have.
I think it is pretty well accepted now that cardio-vascular disease runs in families; that only a small percentage of people run cholesterol over normal on normal diets, and those that do may be helped by diet, but more likely will have to be helped by a drug which will control it as insulin controls diabetes. The perfect drug to control it has not been developed but there is a drug that does stop the body producing cholesterol just short of its synthesis.

The medical profession, and I plead guilty with them, may have unwittingly done a great deal of harm to the dairy industry. To prove how fallacious our concepts may have been may I say that we in Canada use far more butter and have far less coronaries than our neighbours to the south. In talking to representatives of health departments in Great Britain and Europe I learned that no particular diet was stressed. The only thing they did stress was to avoid obesity and to control weight.
In examining the matter more closely we must have in mind that milk has been a food for human beings since life began. Perhaps the health and welfare department could emphasize the importance of milk, cheese and dairy products in general in our economy as being the cheapest sources of calcium, riboflavin and protein.
I wish to dwell for a few minutes on the shortage of trained personnel. We hear so many people say: We will put in a health plan tomorrow and we will cover all dental and medical care. Let me say this. I am wondering what can be done federally by the Department of National Health and Welfare to encourage young people graduating from high schools to enter the fields of dentistry and medicine. Something has to be done if the high standard of dentistry and medicine, the finest in the world, are to be preserved.
It is shocking to learn that only 193 dentists graduated in 1959 compared with 306 in 1950. Nine out of every ten people suffer dental destruction and all children need dental attention before the age of 15. To do all this work in Canada there are only 4,579 dentists in private practice or one dentist for over 3,000 people. In Sweden there is a dentist for every 1,400 and in the United States there is one dentist for every 1,800 people. To meet the need of prevention partially, V.O.P. is training dental hygienists as auxiliary helpers in this field, particularly with regard to the maintenance of healthy mouths in children.
How do we increase the number of dentists to the point of at least keeping the present ratio of dentists to the number of patients? Dentistry schools would have to be enlarged. How are the costs of the course to be met? How are the students going to be able to meet the fees and the other costs of attending university? If they are able to borrow this money, will their earnings be high enough to compensate them for the five years of expensive training plus dental office equipment costing between $7,000 and $10,000 and high rental offices in our cities? Has the

federal Department of National Health and Welfare undertaken any research in this field to learn the answers?
Would a course of four years, with an additional month or two months per year, cut the costs and allow more students to be graduated? The same buildings could be used for the extra two months without any or very little additional cost. I am wondering whether, with our high cost economy in every field, we can allow our educational buildings to stand idle for some months in the year bearing the cost of depreciation and interest charges? I know it will be said that we are short of teachers to carry on any program like this. Yet we met that crisis when the war was on and many of our medical and dental men were away in the services.
There is another point. Should tax incentives be granted until the young graduate has some of his debt off his shoulders? I am speaking particularly of the dental profession although the statements I have made can be applied to many of the other professions, including my own. In the dental field there is now insurance as to dental care with free choice of dentists. Yet what is the use of health insurance or dental insurance if we have insufficient personnel to give the necessary care?
In the medical field it seems to me that everyone wants to be a specialist. In many places there is, I believe, a shortage of general practitioners. Is there anything that can be done to make general practice more attractive to the young graduate? It seems to me that today a young man goes through medical school and rarely meets a general practitioner. Should qualified general practitioners be put on the teaching staffs of universities?
When I went through school all teachers, as I remember, had done some general practice work, the work of the man who has been so aptly described as not only the healer but the friend and counsellor of the family. Too many specialists add to the costs with which the public is already overburdened. In case I may be misunderstood, let me say that the specialist often is able to save lives. Special training is very necessary in many cases, but do not let us lose the general practitioner.
In this field we need many more graduates. Had we not taken in so many doctors from other countries, we would not have sufficient medical personnel today to look after the people of Canada. Again, as I have suggested with regard to dentistry, should the time be cut from six to five years and the course each year lengthened? Should tax incentives be offered young medical graduates? Is the fear of a government dominated health plan scaring away promising young men from the
Supply-Health and Welfare medical and dental fields? Should we encourage young women in our high schools to go into this field, a field that appears to me is being vacated by the young men? In some countries in Europe women doctors are more numerous than men. Perhaps we should learn some of the answers before it is too late and we find ourselves short of necessary medical care. It is my hope that judge Hall and his commission will come up with a sound scheme that will not have to be put in reverse because of hasty, ill-conceived plans.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak on that part of the estimates dealing with the emergency advisory committee and radiation protection. I do not believe anyone today has touched on that part of the program of the minister, and this is a fact I deplore. I believe there is great apathy among the people of Canada and I am sorry to say that it seems there is great apathy in the House of Commons regarding this very important matter. I do not believe it is possible to exaggerate the necessity of having a program for human survival in the event of war. In the newspapers on June 21 last we noted that Douglas Dillon, treasury secretary of the United States, had said that today the Berlin situation is crucial and that a house foreign affairs expert had said that it was possible the United States would be at war with Russia by the end of the year over Berlin.
In the report of the special committee on research I have read that Dr. Stewart said:
I know of no approved shelter in the country, no shelter that has a stamp of approval.
We have had a civil defence organization for ten years and if we continue at the same tempo for the next ten years and war comes we will be totally unprepared. I feel that it is only by a well organized and well

Supply-Health and Welfare thought out civil defence, which will provide fall-out shelters for all Canadians, that this nation will survive a nuclear attack.
With the recent threat of Mr. Khrushchev that he will make a separate peace treaty with east Germany by the end of this year and with the firm warning of President Kennedy and Prime Minister Macmillan that they will resist such a move, hon. members will agree that the tension in the world today has almost reached the cracking point.
While a military defence may have the desired effect against an attack, one must not forget that a well established civil defence is also a great deterrent. If a nation is organized for human survival in the event of a nuclear war, the effect of the nuclear bomb is diminished to the damages caused by the explosion. The greatest damage a nuclear bomb can cause lies in the after effects of the radioactive fall-out. It is of the utmost importance for national survival that precautionary measures be taken at once to safeguard our population. Since 1955 when, at a meeting in Edmonton on August 31, military experts and nuclear war experts warned the nation that the time to act was "now", almost six years have passed.
Although in the last two years a vigorous publicity campaign has been waged by the authorities, there has not been any significant progress toward provisions for human survival. We can say without hesitation that, while the danger of nuclear attack has been brought home to the Canadian people, no concrete measures for the protection of the Canadian people have been taken. There is no purpose in being like the ostrich and burying our heads in the sand. The only way to bring about satisfactory results is through action by the government in enlisting the people in a national defence organization in the same manner as the nation would do if it were at war. The time to act is "now", when we have idle hands, people who are not actively employed in our industry should be enlisted in the same manner as soldiers during a war emergency. There is no point in pretending that we are getting anywhere in our civil defence. We can come to the definite conclusion that if we proceed at the same tempo as we have been proceeding since August 1955 when the nation was told that the time to act was "now", then we will not be ready when war comes. It will then be too late. We must prepare for civil defence now.
In the Toronto Saturday Night of June 10, 1961, there is an article by General F. F. Worthington, former civil defence co-ordinator, comparing what Russia is doing with what Canada is doing. I quote from that article:

Russia:	People are trained and organized
In the U.S.S.R., civil defence training is mandatory for every male person between the ages of 16 and 60 and for every female person between 18 and 50 not in the armed forces or excused for medical reasons. The government provides, maintains and supplies both blast shelters and fall-out shelters.
The basic component of the Soviet organization is the "self-defence group" in heavily populated areas and the "unitary team" in sparsely populated areas.
In peacetime, the duties of both groups, as set out in the Soviet union's civil defence manual under the title "Defence Against Agents of Mass Destruction", are to maintain a constant state of preparation against an attack and to work with the regular authorities in such services as fire prevention.
In the event of an attack, they give first aid to the injured (and veterinary aid to animals), organize the evacuation of the population from destroyed areas and generally work to eliminate the after effects of an attack.
Self-defence groups consist of a chief, his deputy for political affairs, a property manager, communications officer and fire fighting, anti-chemical, emergency rescue, medical (two), shelters, law enforcement and veterinary (in farm communities) teams. Each team is composed of a team commander, four to seven members and a reserve of two men.
Canada:	Survival is up to the individual
Survival for Canadians in a nuclear war is very much a voluntary decision. The government provides no bomb shelters, no fall-out shelters and no supplies or services, apart from essential national services, to aid the citizen. Canadians may, if they choose, build their own fall-out shelters following a government approved plan. Or they may not; no one is compelled to take any precaution against a nuclear war. Those who do choose to take what action they can to protect themselves face a difficult task.
In "eleven steps to survival", publication No. 4 in the blue print for survival series by the emergency measures organization, it is made clear that to be at all effective they must know the effects of nuclear explosions, the facts about fallout, the warning signals (and have a battery powered radio), have a shelter and fourteen days' emergency supplies (100 items), know how (and when) to fight fires; know home aid and nursing, know emergency cleanliness, know how to get rid of radioactive dust, know municipal emergency plans, and finally, have their own plan for their own families.
In all this, the government and government supported agencies provide only the basic information. In many cases, particularly in municipal emergency plans, even the information is as yet unavailable.
As I have just said, in Russia the people are trained and organized. In Canada, survival is up to the individual. It is not sufficient for the government to give good advice to the nation. The government must save the people in spite of themselves. We cannot permit this nation to commit suicide. We must save the people. It is foolish to keep an army just to pick up the pieces after the bomb falls. While first aid is important, it is more logical to avoid casualties and thereby take the sting out of the bomb. As I said before, I feel it is impossible to exaggerate the necessity for a proper civil defence organization. I should

like to say also that if we did have the proper civil defence organization, we would have no unemployment in this country. We could employ anyone who was willing to work and in this way we would have prosperity in peacetime and we would have some assurance of protection in time of war. Let us not kid ourselves. If we did not have insurance agents, we would not buy insurance. If the insurance agents were not paid, we would have no insurance. We will have no proper civil defence organization as long as we are not ready to organize it in a businesslike manner. We know that today the war clouds are all over the world and if we are not careful we will be caught without preparation.
I am sorry to see that there is no more interest in the discussion of this most important item in the estimates. I know the government has advised the people of the dangers; they have told the people what to do, but I believe the people are entitled to more leadership in connection with this matter.

speechtext:
I was greatly interested in hearing the remarks of the hon. member lor St. Boniface. If I have taken his words down correctly he said, "In Russia the people are trained and organized". I do not mean to say very much on the subject of civil defence of our population in case of a nuclear war. However, I should like to inform the hon. member for St. Boniface that, even though the people in Russia may be well trained and organized as to how to defend themselves in case of a potential nuclear war, I am not at all impressed because if nuclear war comes I can assure the hon. member that I do not expect to survive. I can also assure him that if I should be unfortunate enough to survive I would not regard the world as worthy of living in afterward regardless of political organizations or of all kinds of ideologies that may be involved. I consider this to be a whole bunch of nonsense. I think the hon. member might be well advised to consider what he, I and all of the rest of us in the eastern world and in the western world are able to do to prevent this horrible catastrophe from happening.
I have also a brief observation to make on the remarks of the hon. member who preceded the hon. member for St. Boniface, namely the hon. member for Simcoe East. He made a reference to the issue of chronic hospitals. At this point I wish to compliment our government on making available hospital grants and also maintenance grants in respect of the problem of chronic hospitals. I should like to condemn our provincial departments of health in this respect. I completely agree with
Supply-Health and Welfare the hon. member for Simcoe East in his contention that we are operating most uneconomically when we are maintaining in our hospitals many people who ought to be looked after in chronic hospitals.
I believe that our provincial governments are guilty in that they have not supplied any leadership whatsoever with respect to the initiation and the building of hospitals for those who are chronically ill. For a number of years now our federal government have offered to make a major contibution towards the construction of these hospitals; and under our national hospital insurance plan they have also offered to bear what I consider to be a major share of the cost of operation of such hospitals. Yet our provincial governments are evading their responsibilities in this field. This evasion is costing the taxpayers needless amounts of money and it is also causing a great deal of needless human suffering.
Further, I wish to call to the minister's attention at this time especially one particular item. If a man and his wife are each beyond the age of 70 years they are entitled to and receive $55 times 2, namely $110 a month. At the moment either the husband or the wife dies the survivor-and statistics will show that the husband usually dies first and then the widow survives-is left with $55 a month.
I know this issue does not arise in the case of the people who have gone through the means test. However, we have ever so many hundreds of thousands of cases in Canada in which a man and his wife live on the $110 a month. They receive no supplementary benefits. They have been independent people all their lives. They have a minimum amount of savings. They may even have their own home. They may even have an income by way of annuity or pension or what-have-you. However, the moment that one of them dies there is a reduction of 50 per cent in their receipts. This reduction places many of these people in the position in which the survivor-and as I indicated previously in most instances it is the widow-has to submit to the means test in order to receive whatever supplementary benefits are available within the province or within the municipality. I feel that this is most unfair. I feel that we ought to adjust our social security act in order that the survivor, upon the death of the other partner, might be able to receive a little more than 50 per cent of the amount that had been received previously. I know that this issue involves the marginal case.
