I would indeed, Mr. Chairman. I note that the hon. member for Medicine Hat is again in his regular old form. Every time I speak he raises a point of order. However, at this time he did not raise a point of order; he asked a question. 1 would recommend that a man and his wife receive, as they now receive $110 a month. However, if one of them dies, I would recommend that the survivor receive at least $75 a month. I believe this would be a compensation in the case and would eliminate the need for the survivors to subject themselves to the means test and to have their houses and whatever other small annuity or income they might have subjected to scrutiny by welfare officers. I believe it would help to maintain the dignity of these people.
This is an issue that has been called to my attention many and many a time. I pledged my word that I would raise it on the appropriate occasion. I have written letters to the minister and in his replies he always refers me to the ability of the provincial governments and the municipal governments, to deal with the matter, and says that in the case of need they may grant supplementary allowances. I do not think the minister has completely understood the issue involved. All these people know they can apply to the municipalities and provincial governments; that they can submit their case to a means test. However, I feel our basic law is wrong and is weak in this respect, because the basic expenses of maintaining a home for one are not half what they are for maintaining a home for two. The grant should recognize this fact. I think the minister appreciates it. Perhaps our Old Age Security Act ought to be amended in this respect, because as it is now operating we are forcing all kinds of people needlessly to appeal to the municipality or the provincial government, to plead poverty and be humiliated in a way that I think the Old Age Security Act never intended.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to express my thanks to the minister for his resume this morning of the work of his department. I think the minister gave us some very interesting figures to consider. The minister pointed out, as have other hon. members, that the Department of National Health and Welfare is now the second largest spending department of the federal government, being second to the Department of National Defence.


The minister also pointed out that of this $1.6 billion we are spending on health and welfare, 94 per cent is statutory. We know that as our population increases and as people live longer this statutory grant is bound to increase year after year. Of course the figures the minister gave us this morning do not tell the whole story, because in addition to federal spending there is provincial spending.
I do not know whether the minister has available the total amount spent on health and welfare throughout Canada. If he has that figure, I think it would be very useful to have it on Hansard, because I think the federal figure would be much more meaningful if we could consider it against the background of the total cost of health and welfare services throughout Canada. As I have said, these amounts are going to increase year after year and, comprehensive as are our plans for health and welfare, there are still many things we would like to see included in this program.
Some hon. members mentioned portable pensions this morning. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat mentioned that the pension plan should be revised so that the survivor would receive $75 a month instead of the $55 he now receives under the present plan. I think these suggestions are worthy of consideration and are certainly things we would like to include in future plans.
However, because of the kind of economy we have in Canada, we can only have as much as our country can afford. I think this raises the point of whether or not it is possible to organize our expenditures on health and welfare in a more efficient manner than is the case at the present time. According to the figures which the minister gave us this morning, of the $1.6 billion we are spending this year, approximately one quarter will be spent on health. That, of course, is a considerable sum in itself, but we must consider that health is the primary responsibility of the provinces. Therefore the total amount spent on health throughout Canada will be many times that figure.
I have been wondering whether it is possible to find out just what relationship exists, or whether there is any relationship between expenditures on health and expenditures on welfare. I do not know whether the minister's department has carried out any study in this regard, but I think it would be useful to undertake such a study.
Money spent on health must be regarded as an investment, because health means wealth and more production. Health is an important factor in our economic production. Today we have a program of preventive medicine and I wonder whether it might not

be possible to extend that preventive idea a little further than we are at the present time. At the present time we think mainly in terms of vaccines to prevent certain diseases. This morning the minister spoke of physical fitness programs, and these are certainly directly related to health.
I was impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for Simcoe East concerning nutrition and diet. I noted that in the minister's report there is a section on nutrition; we are examining certain foods and setting up certain nutritional standards. However, I think these things should be correlated; I think they all tie in together. I say this because it is my opinion that as a people we Canadians are not healthy. I think we are far too soft physically, mentally, morally and in many other ways.
If we are going to have a program of physical fitness, let us go all out and have a co-ordinated plan, not just a separate plan for physical fitness, a separate plan for nutrition and a separate plan for dieting; let us have a program in which will be incorporated all the factors that contribute to health. I should like the minister to tell us what consideration his department has given to this question.
The minister mentioned another point this morning which was of great interest to me. I refer to radiation protection activities undertaken by the department. The minister said the level of strontium-90 in milk had declined to 9.5 micromicrocuries from 15 points a few years ago. I understand that figure to be an average figure, but I wonder whether the minister could tell us what the latest figures are in respect to the range of levels in the various parts of Canada.
The question of radiation hazard is not confined merely to radiation fall-out. We have now reached the point in our industrial development where atomic energy is coming into greater use. I suggest this raises the problems of hazards from atomic wastes.
I am informed of the decision of the United States court of appeal which prevented the establishment of an atomic power plant at Lacoona beach on lake Erie, some 30 miles southwest of Detroit. That court held that the United States atomic energy commission in issuing a provisional licence for this plant was unmindful of the welfare and safety of the 2 million people who live within a 30 mile radius of that location. I wonder whether, in view of the advent of atomic power in industrial use, Canadian cities and centres might not also be endangered, and should like to know what steps are being taken to forestall this.
As the number of plants using atomic energy increase the disposal and dumping of 90205-6-444
Supply-Health and Welfare wastes and radioactive garbage becomes more and more of a problem. We know that the Ontario hydro electric commission has chosen a site 15 miles north of Kincardine for the establishment of a 200,000 kilowatt atomic power generating plant. I should like to ask the minister what arrangements are being made for the disposal of atomic or radioactive wastes from that plant. I understand that this waste will be disposed of in the waters of lake Huron.
Last November health authorities in Nova Scotia became concerned about the United States atomic energy commission dumping atomic wastes in the ocean 200 miles south of Yarmouth. Individuals who live on the eastern seaboard depend primarily on the products of the ocean-various fisheries-for their livelihood and are very much concerned about the possible effects of radioactive contamination. About that time the Nova Scotian authorities reported this matter to the department of health in Ottawa, but so far as I am aware nothing has resulted since. I should like the minister to comment in respect to this problem when he replies because it seems to me that if radioactive waste dumped into the ocean can be a hazard then the radioactive wastes being disposed of in our inland waters would certainly be a much greater hazard.
Before I resume my seat I should like to thank the minister and his department for the co-operation which was forthcoming a year or so ago in connection with radioactive hazards in my own riding. This radiation hazard occurred in the fluorspar mines at St. Lawrence. Through the co-operation between the minister's department and the provincial departments of health and mines arrangements were worked out whereby safeguards were adopted to protect the health of miners working in that area. It was also my understanding that some arrangements would be arrived at whereby the miners themselves would be provided with some means of monitoring the radioactivity in these mines. I know a lot of miners working there who have been exposed to what they consider the limit and who left because they did not wish to expose themselves any further. I should be grateful if the minister could bring us up to date in respect to what has developed in connection with the radiation hazard in these mines.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister's department is not one with which I have had much dealing or contact and I am, therefore, not in a position to be either critical or flattering in respect to its administration. However, I do wish to ask the minister a few questions and make several

Supply-Health and Welfare comments in regard to one phase of a topic which is considered to be of interest at the present time, and has been of interest for a number of years.
We are all, of course, aware of the situation which has developed in connection with Jean Talon hospital in Montreal, and I am very curious and interested to receive an explanation from the minister as to how grants from the federal government were allocated to this particular institution. I should like to hear about the timing of those grants.
I should like to ask a question of the minister resulting from a certain dissatisfaction with an answer he gave in the house to a question relating to a press release which emanated from his office embodying a speech he made in the constituency of York-Humber while assisting the hon. member representing that riding at a constituency meeting of some kind. I should like to know whether the minister has looked closely at the contents of that speech and whether he does not think he owes his political opponents an apology for embodying in that release very hard hitting, critical and nasty references to both the Liberal and C.C.F. parties. It was a bit of a shock to me that the minister would use his facilities in order to give wide distribution to an out and out political attack such as was embodied in that press release. We appreciate that, politics being what they are, the minister is entitled to have his view that the Liberals are a bunch of rogues and the C.C.F.'ers a scandalmongering group, but when allega-gations and accusations such as those are embodied in a speech emanating from his office one wonders about the coherence of the minister's attitude toward his role as minister. I would appreciate an early explanation in this regard.
Another field in respect to which we deserve some kind of an outline, which I do not believe the minister covered in his introductory remarks, has relation to a fitness council or the rumoured and heralded legislation that was going to be brought forward this session in relation to major support for a physical fitness program. I am sure the minister knows the sad fate of the fitness council which was set up during the war by the previous administration, and how it gradually fell away and finally was put to one side as a useless field of endeavour for the federal government.
A little over a year ago the Prime Minister indicated that the idea of a national fitness council had won his support and that he was going to have federal authorities study the possibility of government participation in such a program. We must assume that this 

is part of the legislation heralded in the speech from the throne. I think we need to hear from the minister as to what form the plans are taking. Anyone who goes back and reads the concluding debate that wound up the affairs of the previous national fitness council and the legislation with regard to it knows that it sickened and died despite whatever merit or purpose it may have had. If we are to get into the field again I think we are entitled to an explanation of what went wrong with the previous legislation. What was wrong with the liaison and the co-operation among all the bodies that made up the former fitness council that led to its demise? If we do not get this information it seems to me we shall be faced with an attempt to do what has already been attempted and found to be a failure.
The aspect of the fitness council that has, of course, more public interest, more fascination, is whatever it may do in the nature of supporting national sport. Here again I think we would welcome from the minister some indication of the role he feels the federal government or his department may play in supporting the national athletic reputation of Canada. My own feeling, and I think that of many of my friends, is that this is not a line of endeavour that should be sponsored by the federal government. And yet increasingly in other nations of the world the national team, whether it be track and field, or team athletics, is becoming an aspect of national pride and national heritage. This being so, a decision has to be made concerning the role the federal government will play. Somehow or other we have never been very bold in determining what that role will be. Since legislation is supposedly coming in this session about it, I think the minister should give us an indication as to the reasons why we should get into this field, or why we should not.
The debate which has taken place in the public mind on this matter has taken place largely on the sport pages of the Canadian newspapers. While I do not think the sport pages are the favourite reading matter of politicians, as someone who checks them with some regularity I can say that in the main the writers of the sport pages of Canada, when they turn to this problem, use an editorial line which is strongly in support of some kind of national endeavour in the field of sport in order to improve the status of Canada's reputation in this regard. Some writers have tried to deal with the very difficult and delicate problem of what role professionalism is to play in this kind of endeavour. In general, no one has worked out a clear-cut approach as to when a sport or an athletic activity becomes of importance

to the national government. We can see this problem in hockey perhaps more than in any other place in that we cannot field a good amateur team in world competition that is a genuinely amateur team according to the traditional classification of amateur, and yet our players have to face units that are organized. developed and sponsored by the states, particularly by the states in the Soviet bloc, where their attitude toward athletics seems to be that, both individual sport and team sports are an important adjunct of life and fully deserve the support of the government.
I think an example we should look at in this particular field is the United States where for many years the state department has backed the sending of United States athletes to different parts of the world, supporting them, providing an appropriation that does not recompense the athletes in terms of professional stipend but ensures that United States athletes are prepared and trained and participate in athletic events around the world.
Of course, the United States, through private auspices, comes forward at Olympic time and at the time of the Pan-American games and provides exceptionally large, or relatively large, sums of money to see that Old Glory is well represented in the athletic fields of the world. One of the reasons the United States can do this without getting into it to the extent that this country can is that the four semester system in their universities leads to a much greater thoroughness and intensity in the kind of training that can be given to athletes of all kinds. In a sense they are subsidized.
I had the pleasure of reading the local newspaper the other day and seeing where three students that I had once taught had graduated from a United States university, and their whole education at these universities was subsidized because of the fact that they were excellent hockey players. Another lad who graduated was an excellent runner. Well, the Americans have built into their universities this promotion or subsidization of their athletes, and so it becomes a support for their international performance. We have not that situation in Canadian universities particularly in track and field sports and in others. Therefore, Canada continues to make a terribly poor showing.
Several weeks ago a bound volume was put out in commemoration of the Olympic games that were held in Rome. If Canadian nationalism is sparked or supported by seeing indications that Canadians have done well, hon. members would be very disappointed in looking at this volume, because continually they would see that athletes from New Zealand, Australia, United States, 90205-6-444i
Supply-Health and Welfare Poland, Hungary, Norway, Finland were all there on the rostrum accepting medals for doing very well. You could see what a reflection of national pride it provided. For Canadians there is almost nothing. I think we have one picture of the famous Ottawa skier, and that is about it. In terms of the actual text of that very thick volume Canadians hardly appear at all. I am not putting it to the minister that this is a very grave or a very serious condition in my opinion, but many people in the country feel that it is, and I am trying to put it to the minister that we should have some indication from this government as to what its views are because whether I, the hon. member for Greenwood or the hon. member for Kootenay West think it is important, it is an issue in much of the country with a certain number of people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. In his research-and it has been very interesting-into the relative success of Canadians and others in international competitions has he discovered whether the success or failure of representative athletes has had any effect in the relative countries on the participation in healthier athletic games?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It has had a tremendous effect, according to what I can find out, because of the tendency today for younger people in particular to search for heroes and symbols of success. When a country does not produce any people who stand in the forefront of world achievement, there is no one to look to for an example. This is one of the difficulties.
Of course, in the Soviet bloc an athletic person of high performance is given a tremendous amount of respect and encouragement and the same, as we know, applies in the United States. We do so too but most of our athletic hero worship at the present time is tending to focus upon activities in two fields, professional hockey and professional football. In the one those who do the chore are mostly Americans and in the other field they are concentrated in a fairly small league of six teams. It is not really international competition in a sense. Good as Jean Beli-veau may be, he is not of world stature such as a runner like Herb Elliott or a runner like Vladimir Kucs or some of the British runners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? In the list of countries which produce many champions he would include Great Britain, would he not?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member with, I would almost say, his British-Israelite zeal should recognize that many people in Britain

Supply-Health and Welfare are greatly disturbed about the situation. They have had the Wolfenden report on the situation which was prepared by the same man who did the study on homosexual psychopaths. He made a study of playground facilities and other sport facilities in Britain and very recently the government there provided more funds for playgrounds and coaching activity in line with the report. If the hon. member wants to look at the British for an example, I would point out that they are very concerned about this problem. It is not surprising to find that in very serious, one might say stodgy, media such as the London Times and the Daily Telegraph, strong support for the old English tradition of games and athletics. We do not seem to have that here.
In concluding this particular aspect of my remarks, I want to say to the minister that I am not advocating that we come out with a policy that strongly supports national endeavour in the field of sport because I am not sure it is a line we should pursue. However, as long as we are going to have an organization like the Canada Council operating in what one might call the field of high culture, we have to recognize that a much larger group of people in Canada strongly believe that in their particular popular culture, sports culture, there should also be leadership. It seems to me that the government has indicated by its acknowledgement in the speech from the throne that it is going to do something about this matter. We would like to know how far it is going to go and what it feels the real urgencies are.
The last point on which I want to touch relates to a very general field that was brought to my mind by the remarks of the medical member for Simcoe East who issued not quite a lament but at least an appeal for the general practitioner. In a couple of contracts I have had with groups of doctors recently I noticed that if you are talking to a surgeon or some other kind of specialist his attitude toward medical insurance is much different from the attitude of the general practitioner. The general practitioner seems to be the doctor who is most against any extension of state operated medical insurance in particular. I should like to refer hon. members to one of the most entertaining articles on doctors that I have ever encountered. It is entitled "Doctors and Politics". It is written by William A. Glaser and it appeared in the American Journal of Sociology for November, 1960. It is filled with a certain amount of sociological jargon but it analyses the medical profession in terms that seem to me to be true. I start with this quotation:
The doctor Is a highly trained expert who uses a codified and technical body of knowledge and skills to solve complicated problems with certainty

and with a high rate of demonstrable success. The politician uses common sense knowledge and personal relations to promote and adjust the demands of competing groups, and his solutions are never permanent and seldom unambiguously successful. From their perspective at the pinnacle of the achievement and reward systems-
He just means that doctors make more money than most people and are looked up to more than most.
-many doctors may look down upon politicians and lay pressure groups as inept and inferior. Medical journals sometimes publish patronizing harangues against politicians. In two surveys doctors and medical students described politicians as people less intelligent, moral and dignified than themselves. The editor of a leading medical journal sums up a viewpoint probably widespread in the profession:
"The doctor's dilemma today emerges from the fact that politics is a dirty-hands business, and medicine has always been a clean-hands profession. Healing and heeling don't go together. Actually, what exponents of pressure-group action by doctors may be saying is that a good end justifies evil means-a doctrine that has been rejected by philosophers since the time of Hippocrates and is shunned by most doctors today in their personal and professional lives."
For all these reasons, the average doctor is not an unusually active participant in campaigns and is neither able nor willing to maintain the year-round involvement in lay politics which yields the greatest political influence.
This analysis of the medical profession and the attitude of the doctor toward politics seems to me particularly relevant at a time when the Canadian Medical Association is trying to give leadership to the doctors in meeting a challenge that is coming from the fact that most political parties have gone on record as supporting a medical insurance scheme that will apply to all or the great majority of the people in the particular jurisdiction in which that party may be interested.
If this analysis is true, it seems to me that the doctors are perhaps peculiarly or particularly inexperienced in understanding or appreciating the pressures that politicians may be under and also the situation into which they are now fully settled. It is for that reason that I would hope that both the provincial medical association and the Canadian Medical Association will continue to do everything in their power to maintain a progressive attitude. If they feel, as their bulletins indicate, that the medical profession can accept this challenge and provide through doctor-supervised plans some complete answer to the medical needs that the people are wanting to have satisfied at the present time, then I think we will tend to be grateful. However, because I believe that this analysis has some sense and is a fairly correct one, I have grave doubts whether doctors as a whole will be able to weather the kind of storms that they will face in producing such a scheme. I would only ask that they

do their best to recognize that, whether or not they produce a scheme that is acceptable to the politicians, they must accept the tact that the country wants a state supported or state sponsored or state led medical scheme for all of the people of the country. It seems to me that as long as they keep trying to come up with something that through cooperation and liaison with government leadership will provide the service, then just so long will they remain in the forefront of their profession both in its practising aspect and its administrative aspect. Of course, it is the administrative aspect that draws them into politics.
One of the answers I always get when I ask both doctors and dentists why they are having difficulty in recruiting at the present time is that there is so much socialism abroad that they cannot attract people into the profession. There is not nearly the urgency to be a doctor or a dentist today because of the fear these professions are going to be taken over by the state. This always seems to me a most incomplete and unsatisfactory response because when one analyses what the medical profession in particular has done, one finds that they have formed into clinics and co-operative groups themselves. They have been doing this for a very long time. The tendency, at least in the part of the country from which I come, is to have a kind of co-operative arrangement among doctors. You rarely find a single doctor operating any more. I am sure there are good reasons for this. There are the expenses that need to be covered, the increasing complexity, the complementary nature of so much that is done in specialized fields in the medical profession.
It seems to me that in answer to that kind of response, I am correct in saying that you, yourselves, in the medical profession have started and have gone along with this trend toward socialism. One of the points I noted two years ago was that the Canadian Medical Association indicated in a statement that one third of the doctors in Canada were on a salary. Surely, if there is that large a proportion of the doctors in Canada on a salary, the whole idea that the trend of the times is undermining recruiting in the medical profession must be haywire. When the percentage is so high, there is every indication that the payment of a salary does not inhibit people from going into the medical profession.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
Would he agree with the statement that one third of the doctors
Supply-Health and Welfare in Canada today came from the socialist medical plan in Great Britain?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Why should I agree with that statement? I do not know whether or not there is any substance to it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This is a statement that has been bandied about quite a bit, and I wondered whether or not the hon. member had read it and agreed with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have not read it. However, I have met a great many doctors from Great Britain in Canada who are great advocates of socialized medicine. I want to tell the hon. member that in the year or so I was attending university in England, I could not find a Conservative anywhere who wanted to ditch the national health plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There still seems to be a number of Conservatives over there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Well, there certainly are and those Conservatives, I point out to the hon. member, are supporting the national health plan. I am sure that his party will be, too, when this subject becomes an election issue.
The last point I wanted to make in relation to this situation of inability to recruit professional men, I think that the difficulty is the cost of education, that is in so far as doctors and dentists are concerned. I agree with the hon. member for Simcoe East that the urgency in connection with dentistry is even greater than in connection with medicine. We are desperately short of dentists in this country. Unless we are prepared to do something to ameliorate the tremendous costs that fall upon people going into these two professions, then I think we are going to run short of practitioners. However, I would hate to believe that the fact we are getting fewer dentists and fewer doctors stems from a situation in which young people today are worried about the encroachment of the state. I would hate to believe that there are not still challenges and worth-while roles for young people in medicine and in dentistry.
I come back to the point again that I feel it is because the training is so long, so expensive and in a way so difficult, it is no longer attractive to very many young people who can get an easier education and a quicker means of earning their living today. The only way we can balance this situation is by giving greater incentives to people who are in training for both those professions.

I would want to be assured that we would not, within 20 minutes, take any chance that there would be a hurried reply on the part of the minister to the very important questions that have been raised by so many members, including members on his own side this afternoon, when we are dealing with expenditures of $1.6 billion. I have remained seated after having spoken earlier today until all other members had an opportunity to make their first remarks in connection with this opening item of this department.
I did not have time this morning under the rules to raise a question that disturbed me after I looked at the white paper presented in connection with the budget this year. I refer to certain tables which relate to the Department of National Health and Welfare found on page 81 of that white paper. In these tables one can find the federal government share of old age assistance, disabled persons' allowances, blind persons pensions and unemployment assistance. The minister and I both represent constituencies in the province of Ontario. Only two or three days ago I observed some of these figures. I rise again because I felt it very important to ask the minister to explain why Ontario, with a larger population than that of the province of Quebec, seems to have received a disproportionate amount in connection with these matching grants related to federal statutes.
I refer to old age assistance in the province of Quebec, the same federal formula being applicable all across Canada, and I notice that the province of Quebec asked the federal government for $10.8 million for these needy people in 1960-61 and received $10.8 from Ottawa. The benign Mr. Frost of Ontario, who has created for himself very sucessfully an image of benevolence, kindness and so on, heads a larger population. I assume, there is in Ontario an equal proportion of needy people in the age group that would


ask for old age assistance, under his administration. Claims are advanced from Ontario to the federal government of only $6.7 million. I thought perhaps the minister would explain why this has occurred. I believe that the opportunities are the same in each province.
Then when one comes to the disabled persons' allowances, with the same understanding that the population in Quebec is smaller than is the population in Ontario, one wonders why under a national basis offer made to Ontario as well as to Quebec, Ontario asked for only $3.9 million of contributions from Ottawa for disabled persons in the year ended March 31, 1961, as compared with $8.5 million given to the province of Quebec.
If one looks at blind persons' allowances, one finds this. According to this latest white paper presented by the Minister of Finance in the province of Ontario with a population, as I repeat, which is larger than that of the province of Quebec, the Frost government seemingly applied for grants in this category of $800,000 compared with applications from the province of Quebec and granted in the sum of $1.5 million. I am not going to deal with the next column of the statistics in the budget white paper.

speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would you encourage me to do so? All right, the next column of statistics refers to unemployment assistance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: By those figures does the hon. member imply that there are more blind people in Ontario than there are in Quebec?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I think perhaps the hon. member for St. Boniface was casting a personal aspersion. But putting that matter aside, I wish to say that I do not believe that. I believe that there is the same entitlement or the same amount of people in Ontario who are needy, or who might be entitled under old age assistance, who are handicapped because of blindness, who perhaps have the physical handicaps that give them entitlement under a law passed by a Liberal government giving disabled persons allowances. I think that in a quantitative way the situation would be the same physically in one province as in another. My point is that these requests for help for these people must be funnelled through provincial agencies. I say that the figures indicate that in Ontario today there seems to be a harsher measure of examination of the entitlement of these needy people than would seem to be

the case in the province of Quebec. I would hope that the minister perhaps later would say something about this matter.
With regard to the column that 1 have been challenged now to speak about, namely that relating to unemployment assistance-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member give us the figures that were in the vote four years ago?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to assure the older parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture that four years ago we had the same government in Ontario as now and no person who needs old age assistance, no disabled person or no blind person can get anything under the legislation that the former Liberal federal government provided unless he has what I would regard as a reasonably kind government in the province. The provincial government must advance to the federal government its request for assistance under this welfare legislation. I say that these figures indicate that the great old province of Ontario, with its big population, seems to fall behind the province of Quebec and every other province relative to population according to the table. I say that Mr. Frost must answer to the old age assistance applicant, to the disabled and to the blind as to why there are fewer successful applicants in Ontario for this kind of benefit which was put on the statute books by the federal Liberal government years ago and why they have less opportunity to derive the benefits than seemingly is possible in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Has the hon. member any figures as to the number of rejections of applications for the social allowances in the province of Ontario?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
May I say this to the parliamentary secretary to the the Prime Minister who is an intelligent man, I know. Surely, it would appeal to him as I think it would appeal to all in the country that these figures speak for themselves. There are surely the same number of needy people between the ages of 65 and 70, relative to population in the province of Ontario as there are in the province of Quebec. I do not imagine that there are more blind people-and I say this in answer to the Prime Minister's parliamentary secretary and to the hon. member for St. Boniface-in Quebec than there are
Supply-Health and Welfare in Ontario. With regard to the disabled and the need for taking advantage of what the former Liberal government provided in legislation of this nature some time ago, in co-operation with the provinces, I say that it is unlikely that the situation en masse would be any different in the province of Ontario than it would be in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit another question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does he know of any specific cases in Ontario in which these applications have been refused?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Of course I do. I am a
resident of the province of Ontario. I am in public life, and I receive from my constituents applications for the benefits that were provided in federal legislation by the former Liberal government that made possible these disability pensions, our old age assistance, these blind pensions, etc.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What are you doing with them?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Because of our constitution I am obliged to say to my constituent that he must utilize the welfare organization of the province in each county of my province. What I am disturbed about is that apparently the welfare officials in Ontario who must know of the availability of the federal grants, are instructed in Ontario at some level on a sterner, harsher basis than would appear to be the situation in connection with the province of Quebec. I observe that the figures show that the province of Quebec has requested from the federal government and the minister and received grants under the same legislation that according to population, are disproportionate. I think this is a very serious challenge.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You mean they want more?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Who wants what?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Quebec; that is what you are saying.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No. I say that here we have legislation for the needy, the most needy people in our land; those who are without assets and without jobs at 65 years of age and before they get the old age security pension automatically. I refer to the people who are disabled, those people who are unfortunately blind, those who are unemployed, and I say that federally we must have a standard that is applied from coast to coast.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Do you not believe that standard applies to blind people right across

Supply-Health and Welfare Canada? Are you saying that blind people in Ontario are not treated as well as blind people in Quebec?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am saying that these figures indicates that going through the crucible-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The which?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The crucible-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What is that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: -of administrative provincial screening-I think the hon. member knows what that means-and considering the attention that must be given administratively under the government of Premier Frost of Ontario, it would appear there is less likelihood of an applicant for old age assistance, a disabled person or a blind person getting as kind or as careful attention as he would get if he happened to reside in the province of Quebec and made his application in that province. The figures bear that out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he mind telling the committee when the hon. member for Essex East will be back?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Not today.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is completely irrelevant. Mr. Chairman, I think I have provided a good summary of what the statistics tell us when we look at page 81 of the white paper attached to the budget of the Minister of Finance presented on Tuesday, June 20.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Five more minutes to go.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think that I have made a very serious indictment-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You have talked it out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: -as to the examination in Ontario of these applications, in kindness and consideration, with regard to what the federal laws provide when I recite-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The crucible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
-the final expenditure figures in all these welfare categories comparing Quebec with the province of Ontario. In his opening statement the minister did refer to the fact that, perhaps for the first time, the old age assistance fund was coming into balance. It is true, Mr. Chairman, that it did come into balance this session, but it came into balance only because of a financial trick typical of the Minister of Finance.
I raised this matter a year ago. Until the budget last year never before has a minister of finance of this country refrained from taking into his budgetary expenditures the deficit
[Br. Broome.]
in the old age security account. This Minister of Finance did not do that a year ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: And as a result of doing that, $28 million was put out of the budget for 1960-61. That was, of course, to achieve his objective of having a $12 million surplus last year when the minister presented his accounts. If one looks at the report of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the old age security fund, one finds that this deficit to which I referred a year ago, which I complained about a year ago, has not been recovered in the budget accounts of 1960-61.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Six o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I say in addition, Mr. Chairman, that we want some of these questions answered by the minister. I think they are very important. We expect a more realistic report from the minister regarding the relationship of his department to the care of human beings across this land. Before we conclude the discussion on item No. 1 I wish to hear the minister's explanation of the relationship between the unemployment insurance fund and sickness. This question has been raised on previous occasions. Are we going to revise the Unemployment Insurance Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Do you mean unemployment insurance, or unemployment assistance?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are we going to have this bankrupt unemployment insurance fund revised during the current session? It has gone down from $900 million to $100 million in four years. In the amendments that will be necessary to revise it, are we going to have the opinion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare? Will we have some recognition of the fact that we should have co-ordination between his department and the labour department and that there should be coverage for those who are unemployed by reason of ill health? Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Shall vote 255 carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I have a few remarks to make on this item, I wonder whether we might call it six o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The Liberals like to hold up the house.
Progress reported.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last evening the house leader indicated what the business would be for Monday and Tuesday. I presume there is no change. I wondered whether we could be told the business for Wednesday.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will repeat the business as announced. On Monday we will start off with second reading of Bill No. C-114, an act respecting the Bank of Canada, followed by the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport. The third item will be the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with the industrial development bank.
I think we will have to see what progress we make on Monday before announcing the
Business of the House
business for Tuesday and Wednesday. It might be that we will continue with the budget debate, but I would prefer to leave it open until the announcement of the business on Monday night.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I just remind the house leader of this fact. Did he not indicate that on Tuesday we would be resuming the budget debate?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I said that was likely, but it is not possible at this stage of the session to determine too far in advance exactly what we will be taking up, because we are not certain how long the session may last.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.

maintopic: ANSWER TO QUESTION

speechtext: The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

maintopic: LABOUR-MANAGEMENT PRODUCTION COMMITTEES
LABOUR-MANAGEMENT PRODUCTION COMMITTEES
speechtext:
1.	When did the Department of Labour first hire field men for the purpose of setting up labour-management production committees?
2.	What was the peak number of persons employed on this type of work during the last war?
3.	What was the low peak, and the date, of the number of persons employed on this type of work in the labour-management co-operation service since the war?
4.	If increases in the number employed on this work have been made since the low peak after the war, what were the numbers involved, and on what dates?
5.	What was the cost of maintaining this service for the years 1944, 1950, 1956, 1960?
Answer by: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of
Labour):
1.	The Department of Labour first hired field men for the purpose of setting up labour-management production committees in 1944, following establishment of the industrial production co-operation board by P.C. 162 of January 18, 1944.
2.	The peak number of persons employed on this type of work during the last war was 20 in 1945.
3.	The low peak of the number of persons employed on this type of work since the war is 11 in 1961.
4.	Not applicable (see answer to 3 above).
5.	The cost of maintaining this service was $72,461 in 1944-45, $127,000 (estimated) in 1950-51, $143,297 in 1956-57 and $162,750 in 1960-61.

Monday, June 26. 1961
